title: Mamdani makes eyebrow-raising claim about Netanyahu protests ahead of NYC visit
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu heads to New York City for the U.N. General Assembly as Mayor Zohran Mamdani walks back his earlier protest-related remarks.
story: 'Fox & Friends' co-hosts react to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's calls to have him arrested under International Criminal Court warrants. Netanyahu addressed Mamdani's remarks during an interview on 'Sunday Morning Futures,' confirming plans to travel to Washington to meet President Donald Trump and attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday he does not plan to attend protests during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s upcoming visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly, while denying that he has ever encouraged New Yorkers to protest the Israeli leader.
The comments come less than two months after Mamdani said New Yorkers had the right to protest Netanyahu’s visit and that he would leave the decision to them.

"I do not have any plans to attend any protest at the UNGA," Mamdani said on Wednesday. "To New Yorkers I have never encouraged them to protest. What I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in this city."
ISRAEL'S AMBASSADOR SAYS NYC’S MAMDANI IS ‘SOWING CHAOS’ AHEAD OF NETANYAHU’S UN APPEARANCE
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks outside Gracie Mansion. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

Mamdani and Netanyahu have clashed over the Israeli leader’s expected New York visit since July, when Mamdani said he had asked his administration to review applicable law to determine whether the city could execute an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu.
The Democratic socialist mayor said in July that New Yorkers had the right to protest Netanyahu’s visit, calling protest "one of the bedrocks of our city."
ISRAELI UN ENVOY BLASTS MAMDANI AS 'CLOWN' OVER CALL TO ARREST NETANYAHU: 'IT'S A STUNT'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that while his office lacks the authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under the International Criminal Court's warrant, he urges the U.S. to do so. (Camara Porter/AdMedia/Sipa USA; Ronen Zvulun/Pool/Reuters)

"It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special, that New Yorkers can express themselves whether they are in support or in opposition no matter on whatever topic," he said during the press conference on July 22.
NETANYAHU ACCUSES MAMDANI OF 'FOMENTING HATE,' SAYS RHETORIC IS MAKING NEW YORK JEWS AFRAID
Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference following a fatal stabbing incident in Times Square in Manhattan, New York, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"And I’ve always said that when we respect our Constitution, we also respect our First Amendment. And here in New York City it will always be a place where you can exercise that," the Mayor added.

Mamdani has repeatedly criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza and accused the country of committing genocide, while voicing support for pro-Palestinian causes. He also skipped New York City’s annual Israel Day Parade on May 31, becoming the first mayor in decades to miss the event.

Mamdani previously called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and "architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

title: Unearthed audio exposes stunning El-Sayed admission about his healthcare pitch
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's 2011 comments reveal his long-standing vision for Medicare-for-all and making healthcare more expensive for wealthier patients.
story: Michigan's 2026 Senate race heats up as progressive nominee Abdul El-Sayed faces intense criticism over his policy platform. Florida Representative Kat Cammack rails against El-Sayed's socialist agenda, comparing his campaign tactics to a used car salesman.

Over a decade before becoming the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged that his vision for healthcare would require different costs for patients depending on wealth status.

"We’re actually just going to give other people access to what you have and make yours more expensive. We’re not asking you to lose access. We’re just making yours more expensive. And not that much so, in fact. We’re making it marginally more expensive," El-Sayed said in a 2011 appearance on the "Sense and Sustainability" podcast.
His resurfaced comments, made as part of a program on inequalities in healthcare, reveal El-Sayed’s long-standing thinking behind his proposed policy changes.
DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Fifteen years later, El-Sayed has made an expansion of healthcare in the U.S. a key part of his platform as he wages a bid to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich.

In particular, he has championed Medicare-for-all, an expansion of the federal program that covers healthcare costs for U.S. citizens over the age of 65 and for some younger recipients with long-term disabilities.
El-Sayed’s plan would expand public coverage for everyone, regardless of income, age or job.

"Medicare-for-all means no premium, no co-pay, no deductible. Doesn’t matter if you get a job, lose a job, turn 26, turn 65, get married, get divorced — it is there for you," El-Sayed said in a post to X earlier this year.
Skeptics of the plan argue it is too expensive and does little to address existing inefficiencies in the American healthcare system.
In 2019, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., took to the Senate floor to blast the idea, calling it a straitjacket solution that would undermine health care quality.
LIZ PEEK: MICHIGAN CAN STOP THE SOCIALIST FEVER RAGE — OR WATCH IT SWALLOW THE SENATE

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks during a primary election night event Aug. 5, 2026, at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

"The [Congressional Budget Office] projects in its report on a single-payer plan that government spending on health care would increase substantially. They go on to say to cover the massive cost of government-run care, income taxes would have to at least double. Income taxes, American families — at least double," Barrasso said.
"Mark my words, Medicare-for-all would soon become Medicare for none."

Despite its hefty price tag, in El-Sayed’s view, the plan is key to ensuring equality of outcomes, even if individual patients are charged differently. He expounded on his design in the 2011 interview.
"We wouldn’t necessarily be ‘stealing from the rich to give to the poor’ in the U.S. because the rich will always have the ability to pay for the care that they need," El-Sayed said.

"The argument would be that everyone’s premiums would go up a little bit. But for the people who actually have premiums now, what they’re losing in terms of the added costs on their health plans are more manageable to them than is the absolute lack of access to healthcare among the people that don’t have it now."
El-Sayed argued that his vision would make costs only marginally more expensive for top earners.
SOCIALISM'S WAR ON SUCCESS HAS A NEW CHAMPION — AND HE’S RUNNING FOR SENATE IN MICHIGAN
Abdul El-Sayed, candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., takes the stage at Mumford High School May 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether it could expand on the costs of El-Sayed’s vision. Having cleared the Democratic primary in Michigan, El-Sayed will face Republican challenger Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the state's Nov. 3 general election.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: AI hysteria has a Y2K problem — and the stakes this time could be far higher
summary: Critics compare AI regulation fears to Y2K and climate change hysteria, arguing the tech industry can self-correct without sweeping government action.
story: Heritage Foundation technology analyst Annie Chestnut Tutor  and Junk Science publisher and founder Steve Milloy tell Fox News Digital  AI can benefit Americans if 'built right' rather than treated as a doomsday scenario.

Washington’s growing alarm over artificial intelligence is beginning to echo Y2K, experts say, when dire warnings of technological catastrophe prompted a massive scramble to avert failures that ultimately proved far less severe than feared.

"You could draw all sorts of scary scenarios with Y2K as well. The financial system was just going to collapse because people had not written their programs for the year 2000. I had been writing programs in the 1980s for the government, so I'm well aware of the program," Junk Science publisher and founder Steven Milloy told Fox News Digital.
"But of course, the tech industry knew about the problem, and to the extent that was a real problem, took action to fix it. The same can happen with AI," Milloy added.
RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION
President Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order on AI in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., Dec. 11, 2025. (Al Drago/Reuters)

Y2K was a computer bug that raised fears systems could fail when the calendar changed from 1999 to 2000. The U.S. spent an estimated $100 billion, $200 billion adjusted for today's inflation, in preparing for the problem, according to a 2000 Senate report.
When the new millennium arrived, there were few major disruptions.

President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and Democrats cry foul before midterm elections.
DEMOCRATS EMBRACED AI’S GROWTH BEFORE TRUMP CAME ALONG — NOW THEY WANT TO SLOW IT DOWN
"Democrats are capitalizing on the fears of Americans that angst over AI," Heritage Foundation technology analyst Annie Chestnut Tutor told Fox News Digital.

Democrats are increasingly calling for government guardrails on AI, citing potential threats ranging from job losses and inequality to risks to democracy and humanity. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, for instance, wrote in April that AI "kills jobs, equality, connection, democracy and maybe the human race."
But the apocalyptic warnings are not coming only from Washington.

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company over concerns about the race toward self-improving AI, warning that its developers are "gambling with our lives" and that such systems could potentially "kill us all by the end of the decade."
SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE
Y2K sparked similar fears, as warnings spread of potential power-grid failures, disruptions to air travel and air-traffic control, and even predictions that planes could fall from the sky.

The Trump administration has backed targeted safeguards, including AI-powered cyber defenses for critical infrastructure, criminal enforcement against AI-enabled hacking and proposed measures to limit AI-driven child exploitation.
Tutor offered a nuanced Y2K comparison, arguing that the episode showed how technological risks can be addressed before they become potentially catastrophic.

"The reason now, like, we all laugh about Y2K is because actually software engineers and, like, financial analysts, they've worked really hard to ensure that the catastrophic incidents [didn’t] happen," Tutor said.
AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK
"I think the same thing could happen with AI," she added. "If AI is built right, it can be more beneficial to Americans than the doomsday scenario."
Democrats are increasingly calling for government guardrails on AI, citing potential threats ranging from job losses and inequality to risks to democracy and humanity. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Milloy said the Y2K comparison also fits a pattern he sees with climate change, with dire warnings of an existential threat followed by calls for sweeping government intervention.

Climate warnings have likewise been framed in apocalyptic terms, including predictions that entire nations could be wiped out by global warming, Arctic summer ice could disappear within years and Glacier National Park’s glaciers would vanish by 2020.
FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

"There are a lot of parallels between climate hysteria and AI hysteria," Milloy said. "Climate was existential. It was going to destroy the planet, and by implication, humanity. As we learned last week, AI is going to destroy humanity also on a very short time frame."
Milloy argued that while lawmakers are crying foul, they have not established enough specific evidence of catastrophic AI scenarios to justify sweeping restrictions.
Trump has responded to AI warnings by calling them a "hoax," reviving the language he has used for years to dismiss climate change concerns.
"Give me a real-life practical scenario of how this can happen," he said. "And then if you know what the scenario is, then you can stop it."
DAVID MARCUS: BIG TECH INVENTED AI DOOMSDAY TO DUCK REAL LIFE PROBLEMS
President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority. (iStock; Rob Newell - CameraSport via Getty Images)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Milloy warned that overly broad regulation could carry its own cost by slowing technological advances before their benefits are fully understood.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The opportunity costs are potentially huge," Milloy said, pointing to potential AI-assisted advances in medicine and productivity while acknowledging that their ultimate scale remains unknown.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Scandal rocks Utah campus as student who celebrated Charlie Kirk’s death sparks online firestorm
summary: A viral photo of a "Happy Kirkiversary" cake sparked a University of Utah probe into two College Republicans accused of doxxing a fellow student.
story: Charlie Kirk's mock death celebrations on college campuses face criticism from Greg Gutfeld and his panel. The host is joined by Trace Gallagher, Charles Payne, Jamie Lissow, and Kat Timpf to analyze the controversial 'Kirkiversary' trend marking a fake September 10th anniversary. The guests debate the offensive nature of these student events and discuss campus free speech.

A college student photographed with a cake mocking Charlie Kirk's death is at the center of a campus controversy that has prompted the University of Utah to investigate two College Republicans for charges of misconduct after one posted the photo online.

On Sept. 10, 2026, the one-year anniversary of the conservative activist's public murder, a woman approached a group of College Republicans at an event on the school's campus and presented them with a cake. The words "Happy Kirkiversary" were written in red icing on the white cake.

Students Riley Beesley, the chairman of the school's College Republicans chapter, and Rylie Barnes, also a member of the group, took exception to the stunt on a campus less than an hour's drive from another college campus where Kirk was assassinated last year.
Barnes posted a photo of the cake to her X account, and it quickly went viral and led to an anonymous X user identifying the student as Sara Larsen.
Sara Larsen holds a cake that says "Happy Kirkiversary" on Sept. 10, 2026, at the University of Utah. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)
UNIVERSITY OF TENNESSEE CONDEMNS FLYERS APPEARING TO CELEBRATE CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION
The school's College Democrats responded by saying Republicans are "waging a campaign of hate" against them.
On Tuesday, the university sent emails to Beesley and Barnes requesting closed-door meetings Wednesday morning with its Student Rights and Responsibilities office.

"We received information that, if accurate, may go against this priority and the policy on Student Rights and Responsibilities, and I would like to meet and hear your perspective," says a copy of one of the emails, obtained by Fox News Digital. "The report is regarding an incident that happened on or about September 11, 2026 and allegedly involves you attempting to doxx another University of Utah student over a political issue."
The email was sent by the office's assistant director, Jose Morales Diaz.
"Doxxing" is the act of publicly revealing, usually online, the personal information of another person, typically with the intent of causing harm to that individual.

"We will talk about the information our office received, and you will have an opportunity to give your perspective of the incident if you wish. We will also talk about possible next steps, such as resolutions and educational or restorative measures if appropriate," the email said.
A sign at the entrance of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, Utah, on Sept. 9, 2011. (Getty Images)
30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS
The emails also prohibited the students from recording the meetings. But shortly before the meetings were scheduled to take place, the university abruptly canceled them, according to Beesley.
Diaz did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"We found it distasteful, vile, and disgusting. Parents, alumni, students and donors deserve to know about the radical political ideologies festering on college campuses in Utah," Beesley told Fox News Digital of the cake incident.

"Given today's political climate, mocking or expressing support such as this should be taken incredibly seriously and the public sphere has a right to know about the lack of morality being observed among young Democrats and those on the left."
He strongly condemned doxxing, and said his group had nothing to do with the release of Larsen's information. He also condemned political violence.

Conservative political activist Charlie Kirk, founder of Turning Point Action, speaks during a meeting on the campus of the University of Arizona in Tucson on Oct. 17, 2024. Turning Point Action, a conservative campaign group, is working to get Republican Donald Trump elected and has hired thousands of canvassers to get out the vote. (OLIVIER TOURON/AFP via Getty Images)

"We're observing patterns where those on the left find it comical to make threats, have normalized silencing opposing political viewpoints, and avoid accountability or consequences for glorifying murder," he said. "This must end."
CARNEGIE MELLON 'DEEPLY CONCERNED' BY PROFESSOR'S 'HOSTILE AND THREATENING POSTS' ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH
The university told Fox News Digital it can't comment on student disciplinary action, citing federal law.
But Wednesday night, the school released a statement about the ongoing controversy, which has been going viral online for days and has become a national news story.

"In recent days, a dispute between political groups on the University of Utah campus has resulted in allegations of harassment, threats, and the inappropriate sharing or amplification of personal information. The University of Utah is reviewing these accusations consistent with established policies, due process and applicable law," the statement said.

"As we conduct this review, the university will continue to simultaneously protect freedom of expression and the safety of our students. Calls to harm someone, including electronic harassment and inappropriate sharing of information, are not protected by free speech," it continued.
The school also urged the College Democrats and College Republicans groups on campus to convene with leadership in an attempt to better understand one another.
It also condemned violence.
COLORADO TPUSA CHAPTER ENROLLMENT 'FLAT' AFTER ELDERLY SUPPORTER WAS STRICKEN BY STUDENT WITH TACO BELL CUP
A University of Utah student was caught on camera allegedly threatening a conservative group of students. (Reawaken USA)
Beesley was subject to an alleged violent threat on campus earlier this year, when a person threatened to "Kirk" him.

"It was January 12, we were outside tabling and engaging in debates in a format similar to those organized by, let's say, Turning Point USA," Beesley told Fox News Digital at the time. "And soon after [he] declared to us, 'you should die,' followed by, 'I am going to Kirk you,' which you could only think that means I'm either using your imagination going to shoot you or kill you."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Dean Stewart, then 21, was arrested following the incident. Criminal proceedings against him are ongoing, Beesley said.

An X account with the name Sara Larsen made a post on Sept. 11, 2026, apologizing for the cake stunt. Fox News Digital could not independently verify whether the account owner is the student embroiled in the controversy.

"Upon reflection, it was wrong for me to celebrate, or perpetuate the celebration of, Charlie Kirk’s death. I apologize for doing so sincerely. Nobody should be murdered or persecuted for their speech," reads the tweet — the only post present on an account with 311 followers that was created in February 2017.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Former GOP whip, Arizona Sen Jon Kyl dead at 84
summary: Former Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl, an Arizona Republican who served nearly three decades in Congress, has died at age 84 following a battle with dementia.
story: Former Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl, R-Ariz., is dead at the age of 84, his family announced Thursday.
Kyl was first sworn in to the Senate in 1995, retiring in 2013. He briefly returned to the Senate in 2018 after former Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., died.
Kyl announced he was stepping away from public life in December 2025 after receiving a diagnosis of a neurological disease that resulted in his development of dementia.
Before his election to the Senate, Kyl was a member of the U.S. House of Representatives from 1987 to 1995.
AN EMPTY US CAPITOL AFTER MCCAIN’S DEATH IS SOBERING REMINDER THAT THE CLOCK IS TICKING
Sen. Jon Kyl, R-Ariz., departs the weekly Republican policy luncheon on Sept. 25, 2018, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Former Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who appointed Kyl to fill McCain's seat in 2018, paid his respects to the former senator in a Thursday post on X.

"Jon Kyl gave Arizona nearly three decades of principled, thoughtful leadership — and he gave me something just as valuable: his mentorship and friendship. I'll miss him deeply. Rest in peace, Senator Kyl," Ducey posted.
Former Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Ariz., who served in the Senate with Kyl, also paid homage to the late lawmaker.

"Arizona has lost a giant. Jon Kyl was one of the most diligent and effective public servants Arizona has ever had. I was honored to follow him in the U.S. Senate, where his example of seriousness, integrity and devotion to public service was known to all. Cheryl and I send our deepest condolences to Caryll and the entire Kyl family," Flake posted on X.

Former Sen. Jon Kyl, left, and Bruce Babbitt, right, former Arizona governor and secretary of the interior, wave to the crowd as they are recognized during Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey's state of the state address Monday, Jan. 14, 2019, in Phoenix. (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin)
Flake also gave remarks to reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.

"I admired him from the get-go, when he was back in the House, and I was in Arizona. When I ran for office, he gave me the best advice I ever got. He said that, when you get back to Washington, make sure your family is aware of what you're doing, is involved in it. He said they will either resent it or revel in it. And that was the best advice I got, because we tried to follow that. And he was just… in addition to being an extremely effective public servant, he was a good man. And I think that that shined through," Flake told reporters.
TILLIS' RETIREMENT ANNOUNCEMENT DRAWS REACTIONS FROM TRUMP CRITIC JEFF FLAKE, BERNIE SANDERS: 'A CULT'

"For Arizona, you know, every Western state has similar issues; water issues, public land issues. And Jon took that on," Flake said. "That's the workhorse in him. I think he did nine Indian water settlements during his time, which has allowed the Indian tribes in Arizona to have the water they need and also for the state to grow sustainably," Flake continued. "And then also, in terms of his legal mind and his, you know, concern about the Supreme Court. And he was asked after he had left Congress to sherpa certain nominees through, and he was extremely effective in that because he had the respect of his colleagues."
Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Ariz., accompanied by his wife Cheryl, leaves the Capitol in Washington, Tuesday, Oct. 24, 2017, after announcing he won't seek re-election in 2018. (AP)
Flake also revealed that he last spoke with Kyl just before the late senator announced his dementia diagnosis.

"December of last year he put out a statement. I had talked to him just before that. And it was a wonderful conversation. He was very much aware of all that the state had gone through, and I made sure to tell him how appreciative all Arizonans are of what he did for the state and what he did for the country. And, he was so devoted to his wife, Carol, and his family, and the state of Arizona," Flake said.
Flake also commented on the unique situation that arose when Kyl was appointed to replace McCain.

"When Senator McCain passed away, there was an appointment, and he served out that term for the last few months. So I got to serve with him in the Senate and also jokingly be the senior senator to him, which I didn't deserve. But it was just a wonderful relationship throughout," Flake said.

summary: Siddharth Jawahar, an illegal immigrant from India, was sentenced to 11 years for a $35 million Ponzi scheme that victimized Travis Kelce and NBA stars.
story: A multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme lists Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce as a victim. Investment manager Siddharth Jawahar faces an 11-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors reveal Jawahar swindled victims out of more than $35 million through Swift Art Capital LLC, using new investor money to fund an extravagant lifestyle of private jets and luxury hotels.
The mastermind behind the multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme that even victimized NFL star Travis Kelce is an illegal immigrant from India.

Thirty-eight-year-old Siddharth Jawahar was sentenced to 11 years in prison this week for running a $35 million investment wire fraud scheme. At his sentencing, Judge Zachary Bluestone said that through his investment company, Swiftarc Capital LLC, Jawahar "weaponized" investors' trust, resulting in "massive" losses for the victims.

Jawahar raised more than $35 million from investors between 2016 and 2023 and only invested roughly $10 million of that total. He spent the remainder funding personal luxuries, including private jet charters, upscale apartments in Austin and New York, high-end dining, shopping sprees at clothing stores and exclusive private club memberships. He has now been ordered to pay $31.35 million in restitution to his victims.

But that is not the end of Jawahar’s legal issues. He may also be subject to deportation. According to the Department of Justice and a court document reviewed by Fox News Digital, Jawahar is an illegal immigrant from India who has been living in the U.S. since 2005.
TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

Travis Kelce #87 of the Kansas City Chiefs was officially named as one of the victims in a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme masterminded by Indian illegal immigrant Siddharth Jawahar. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images)

He also tried to get his sister to remotely wipe his iPhone to hide evidence, the DOJ said.
Jawahar pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in January 2026.

Among Jawahar’s victims was Kelce, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end who recently married pop superstar Taylor Swift, and several NBA players, including Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Mason Plumlee. The DOJ said Jawahar’s victims resided in Missouri and elsewhere.

Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce (87) looks on before kickoff against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL game at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on Oct. 7, 2024, in Kansas City, Missouri. (Cooper Neill/Getty Images)

Jawahar also managed 17 additional entities that he utilized during his scheme.

title: Historic newspaper gives El-Sayed a savage rebuke for hiding his past while endorsing his opponent
summary: The Detroit News endorsed Mike Rogers for Michigan's Senate race while blasting Abdul El-Sayed for deleting thousands of past social media posts.
story: Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed dodged Fox News Digital’s question about whether Hasan Piker will campaign with him as he entered a meeting with Democratic senators at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters.

A top newspaper in battleground Michigan is skewering left-wing Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed over past radical rhetoric as it endorses Republican rival former Rep. Mike Rogers in a crucial midterm showdown.
The race between El-Sayed and Rogers to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is a must-win battle for the Democrats as they try to recapture the Senate majority from the GOP.

The Detroit News, which has the second-largest newspaper circulation in Michigan, charged in its endorsement of Rogers that El-Sayed "has worked so hard covering his tracks leading up to this Senate race that it's impossible to know who he really is or where he would stand in the Senate."
WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POLLING

The Detroit News, Michigan's second-biggest newspaper by circulation, endorsed Republican Senate nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers, left, in his race against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images; Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)

He's taken down roughly 100 YouTube videos that paint an unflattering picture of him and his cultural views," the conservative-leaning newspaper argued. "A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted to be the same person after Election Day as he was on the campaign trail."
As he runs for the Senate, El-Sayed has removed or archived thousands of past social media posts and older podcast/YouTube videos.

Some of those past comments include floating the idea of abandoning fireworks on July 4th, suggesting replacing the nation's Second Amendment with the "right to have health care," and one-time support for the "defund the police" movement.
El-Sayed, who was captain of his high school football team, also criticized football's ties to toxic masculinity and a "bro culture."

title: Powerful teachers' unions share striking link with states struggling to teach kids to read
summary: A Progressive Policy Institute study links strong teachers unions to weaker student literacy, with eight of the 10 lowest-scoring states affected.
story: Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves discusses the state's dramatic rise in national education rankings, detailing the key literacy and reading reforms behind the success. Reeves credits the state's structured literacy laws and focused reading programs for transforming the educational system.

States with stronger teachers' unions tend to have weaker literacy performance and have adopted fewer of the policies credited with improving reading outcomes, according to a new analysis from a center-left think tank.

Eight of the 10 states to score among the worst in the Progressive Policy Institute’s (PPI) assessment of early-literacy policies were home to powerful teachers' unions. Among the top 60% of states in terms of early-literacy policy scores, only four had strong teachers' unions.

Mississippi, Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, South Carolina and Indiana, all Republican-leaning states with weak unions, were among the states with the best literacy outcomes. Maine, New York, Illinois, Hawaii, Washington and Rhode Island, blue states, were among the worst.
ARKANSAS STUDENTS OUTPERFORM NATIONAL AVERAGE AFTER UNIVERSAL SCHOOL CHOICE EXPANSION, GOVERNOR SAYS

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, speaks during a rally outside the U.S. Department of Education headquarters in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, March 13, 2025. President Donald Trump was sued by a group of mostly Democratic-led states over his alleged plan to effectively dismantle the U.S. Education Department by slashing its workforce in half. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The pattern isn't universal. Maryland, a blue state with a strong teachers' union, has posted strong reading results, while South Dakota, a red state with a weaker union, has struggled. The differences suggest union strength and party control alone don't explain states' reading performance.

Rachel Canter, PPI’s director of education policy, conducted the analysis with colleagues by comparing teacher-union strength rankings with states’ early-literacy policy scores. Canter is also one of the people behind the slate of educational reforms in Mississippi that propelled the state from among the worst in the country for educational outcomes to among the best.
"Democrats, however, don’t often ask me how to replicate Mississippi’s success," Canter said. "They ask if it’s possible at all, given the power of teachers’ unions in their home states."

Teachers' unions, according to Canter, exert massive amounts of influence over both educational policies and how those policies are implemented in the classroom. This can make schools in states with stronger unions slower to adapt to challenges or to adopt new, better methods.
TEACHERS UNION FACING YEARS OF DEFICITS SEEKS TO BECOME OREGON'S LARGEST PAC, INTERNAL DOCUMENTS SHOW

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, speaks during the Democratic National Convention at the United Center in Chicago, Aug. 22, 2024. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Mississippi’s reforms, among other things, added kindergarten-through-third-grade screenings, literacy coaches, individual reading plans and held back third-graders who failed the state reading test. The state reinforced those measures with science-based reading instruction, increased teacher training and tougher licensing requirements.
Tweaks to teaching like these can be difficult to achieve in states with influential teachers' unions, with labor reps arguing that the changes place undue burdens on educators.
ILLINOIS DEMOCRATIC GOVERNOR BUCKS TEACHERS' UNIONS IN SUPPORT FOR STATEWIDE CLASSROOM PHONE BAN

Chicago Teachers Union Vice President Jackson Potter speaks at a rally outside Chicago Public Schools headquarters, Feb. 26, 2026. (Antonio Perez/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Many of the states that underperformed in the Progressive Policy Institute’s study also have Democratic leadership. Teachers’ unions spend hundreds of millions of dollars every electoral cycle on electing Democrats and pushing left-of-center policies.
"States dominated by Democrats have been slower to embrace similar reforms," Canter said. "Organized labor might explain some of this gap."

Multiple GOP-led Southern states have adopted educational reforms similar to those introduced in Mississippi. Those same states dominated the Progressive Policy Institute’s rankings of the states with the best student literacy.

title: Trump’s $5K checks could join stack of past unfulfilled promises, former Congress budget chief warns
summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 tariff checks and DOGE savings promises are unlikely to arrive, says former CBO Director Douglas Holz-Eakin.
story: A top economist who worked to set government economic policy is warning the President Donald Trump’s plan to send cash payments to Americans likely won’t pan out, and that the plans have serious implications for the American Dream.
President Donald Trump's latest cash promise to Americans is unlikely to come to fruition, just like others before it, an economist and former congressional budget hawk told Fox News Digital.

"So the president has promised a lot of checks, the most recent being $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold on to the House and Senate. We ever going to see these? Well, I don't think so," said Douglas Holz-Eakin, president of fiscal policy think tank American Action Forum.
Holz-Eakin previously served as the director of the Congressional Budget Office and as the director of domestic and economic policy for late Republican Sen. John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign.
TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'

Trump has repeatedly defended tariffs as a key pillar of his economic agenda, saying they will bring manufacturing back to the United States and generate revenue as Republicans seek to hold Congress in the November elections. (Mike Kropf/Getty Images)

"The DOGE checks were never realistic because DOGE was never going to save that much money," said Holz-Eakin in reference to the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency's sweeping layoffs and budget cuts to federal agencies.
He continued: "And the tariff checks were never that realistic because [Trump] didn't have the authority to issue the checks, and that's actually true of all of these promises."
Holz-Eakin also mentioned the Trump administration's recently proposed plan to give $9,000 checks to stay-at-home mothers likely won't come through either.

"Trying to get money to stay at home moms for childcare, there's a route to that, but it's gonna be tough ... we'll see if they actually pull it off," he said. "So, I would be skeptical that any of these checks are gonna be in your mailbox very soon."
The internationally-known economist likened the Trump administration's fiscal policy to that of former President Joe Biden's Democratic administration.

"I think we've seen two successive administrations get themselves in the following position: inflation is too high and wages aren't keeping up with it. Well, that's failing at the American dream," Holz-Eakin explained.
THE FED JUST THREW A WRENCH IN TRUMP'S MIDTERM ECONOMIC MESSAGE

He said that getting inflation under control was the first step in restoring order, as well as being "utterly supportive" of the Federal Reserve, which Holz-Eakin says is working to achieve that goal.

The Fed hiked interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years, and signaled that more rate increases could be coming. This comes despite Trump's push to have the world's most powerful central bank lower interest rates to lessen the monthly burden on Americans seeking home and auto loans.
The U.S. national debt hits $40 trillion for the first time and there is little relief in sight. (Fox News)

"Inflation remains elevated," the Federal Open Market Committee said in a post-meeting statement. "Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
"You need to have, I think, a more vibrant economy, and this economy is doing okay, but it's putting up with a lot of headwinds," said Holz-Eakin.
He named specific Trump administration policy decisions he says are to blame for the lackluster economy, which has burdened the middle class as grocery prices continue to rise.

"The first headwinds were tariffs, second headwinds were the oil prices and fight with Iran, and we need to get past those battles, and let the economy just go, and ... that would be a better environment for the families," he told Fox News Digital.
CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100

President Donald Trump presents Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell with what he called a list of cost overruns for the Federal Reserve’s $2.5 billion headquarters renovation project on July 24, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
As for overall fiscal policy, Holz-Eakin says he's worried that the country is going in the wrong direction when it comes to economic and fiscal policy.
"I'm a former director of the Congressional Budget Office. I have to every day get up and look at the books and wonder, 'how's this going to add up?'" he said. "And right now it doesn't add up."
"We're $41 trillion in debt. The deficit is $2 trillion every year and it's getting larger. You can't just keep putting people on the on government programs. It won't add up."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He proposed a fix — reverting to "old-school conservative" politics.

"I'd like to see a bit of a U-turn that got the debt under control, didn't spend quite so much money, and got through this without having to raise our taxes. So, that sounds like an old-school conservative plan to me, but that's not what we're seeing right now."
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Trump's economic promises, but did not hear back at time of publication.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Federal judge ties ICE agents' hands with ruling on warrantless Southern California arrests
summary: A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking ICE from carrying out warrantless immigration arrests unless the target is likely to escape before a warrant is obtained.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse reports from Los Angeles on Assembly Bill 1896, legislation that restricts police departments and local governments from hiring individuals who conducted federal immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump.

A federal judge with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California issued a preliminary injunction to block the U.S. government from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests in the district unless the arrestee is deemed likely to escape before a warrant can be procured.

"Defendants are enjoined from enforcing their policy and practice of making warrantless civil immigration arrests in this District without a prearrest individualized determination by the arresting agent or officer of probable cause that the person being arrested is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, as required by 8 U.S.C. 1357(a)(2) and 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(c)(2)," the order signed by U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong reads, in part.
Frimpong was nominated by former President Joe Biden during his White House tenure.
EXCLUSIVE: 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11, ICE SAYS MORE THAN 2K KNOWN OR SUSPECTED TERRORISTS HAVE BEEN DEPORTED
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents walk a detainee out of the Ventura County Government Center in Ventura, Calif., on July 27, 2026. (Blake Fagan / AFP via Getty Images)

"Mere presence within the United States in violation of United States immigration law is not, by itself, sufficient to conclude that a person is likely to escape before a warrant for arrest can be obtained," the judge's order notes.
The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California encompasses the following counties: Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties.
ANGEL DAD REBUKES DEMOCRATIC LAWMAKERS OVER SANCTUARY POLICIES AFTER DAUGHTER KILLED BY TWICE-DEPORTED FELON

The badge of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent is seen as they patrol the halls of immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building on June 9, 2025, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"This ruling is one of the most important decisions to date in the community’s effort to end the federal government’s cruel and illegal practice of abducting people and separating them from their families," ACLU Foundation of Southern California senior staff attorney Mayra Joachin declared in a statement.

"By requiring immigration agents to follow the law’s requirement to make escape risk determinations before they can arrest someone without a warrant, this court order should put an end to hundreds — if not more — of unlawful arrests that continue throughout Southern California. We will closely monitor compliance with this court order, and expect the federal government to abide by it," Joachin added.
MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS

The Department of Homeland Security provided Fox News Digital with the following statement on Thursday: "ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Political insider turns anti-incumbent table on 8-year Dem in key Senate race: 'Hasn't delivered'
summary: John E. Sununu flips the anti-incumbent script on Chris Pappas, calling him ineffective on highway funding as the NH Senate race hits toss up.
story: Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the 2026 Republican Senate nominee in New Hampshire, takes aim at Democratic rival Rep. Chris Pappas in a Fox News Digital interview in Concord, N.H. on Sept. 14, 2026.
CONCORD, N.H. - A Republican running to flip a blue Senate seat in a crucial battleground state is flipping the script on the Democrats' anti-incumbent argument.

Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the GOP Senate nominee who's running to return to Capitol Hill after 18 years away, charges that his Democratic rival, Rep. Chris Pappas, has "been in Washington for 8 years and hasn't delivered for New Hampshire."

Sununu and Pappas are facing off in the midterm election in the battle to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen in a race that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if Republicans hold their control of the Senate.
"He has attempted very little in Congress. He's accomplished even less," Sununu said in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview this week, as he blasted Pappas, a four-term congressman.
THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DETERMINE IF REPUBLICANS HOLD THE SENATE
Former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire celebrates his Republican Senate nomination victory, in Manchester, N.H., on Sept. 8, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

Sununu was interviewed ahead of a move by the Cook Political Report, a top nonpartisan campaign handicapper, to shift the race in New Hampshire from lean Democrat to toss-up. Earlier this month, another leading nonpartisan handicapper, Inside Elections, also changed their rating to a toss-up.

It was a rare move in favor of the Republicans amid a political cycle where the GOP is facing traditional political headwinds for the party in power in D.C.. Republicans are also confronting an extremely rough political climate fueled by persistent inflation, soaring fuel prices due to the ongoing war with Iran, and President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings.
So what's Sununu's secret sauce?

Part of it is his last name, which is a political brand in New Hampshire. Sununu's father, John E. Sununu, served six years as governor before heading to Washington, D.C., as then-President George H.W. Bush's White House chief of staff. And one of his younger brothers, Chris Sununu, recently served eight years as governor before taking a break from politics.
But also boosting Sununu, his strategy to blast Pappas as a do-nothing member of Congress during another anti-incumbent election cycle, which is a turn of the tables on the Democrats' playbook.
CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE BATTLE FOR THE SENATE

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, a U.S. Senate candidate, is joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren of neighboring Massachusetts, at a campaign stop in Dover, N.H. on Sept. 5, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

"He's been on the Transportation Committee for eight years, and New Hampshire is dead last in highway funding in New England. That hurts New Hampshire. His ineffectiveness is doing damage to the state because we're not getting the support we need from Washington," Sununu claimed.

While it doesn't rank dead last in every single metric or category, New Hampshire receives some of the lowest total and per-capita levels of federal funding for roads, highways and bridges of any state in the country, according to federal and state figures.

Pappas, earlier this year, introduced the Highway Fair Share Act, a bill to increase federal funding for infrastructure and transportation projects for New Hampshire by requiring that each state receive at least 0.5% of the total federal-aid highway formula funding.
Pappas and the rest of the all-Democratic congressional delegation in June highlighted $9 million in federal funding for New Hampshire projects.

"Chris Pappas has led efforts to expand healthcare benefits for 3.5 million veterans, bring high-speed internet to towns across New Hampshire, put more money back in the pockets of working parents, and secure millions of dollars to improve and repair roads, bridges, and buildings," Pappas Campaign Manager Rachel Petri told Fox News Digital, as she shared a long list of funding accomplishments by the congressman.

Petri said, "Chris is rated among the most effective and bipartisan lawmakers and his record stands in stark contrast to John Sununu’s record of voting to cut Medicare, leading efforts to privatize Social Security, and backing Donald Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran."
Sununu's anti-incumbent argument is a bit ironic, considering he spent six years in the House and a term in the Senate before losing a rematch with then-former Gov. Shaheen in the 2008 election.
Looking back at his years on Capitol Hill, Sununu touted his record "of writing and passing legislation under Democrat presidents, Republican presidents, a Democrat Congress, Republican Congress."

But he also emphasized, "I've been in the private sector for the last 16 years. That's a good thing, working for tech firms and small businesses, the Waterville Valley ski area [the Sununu family has had a controlling interest in the resort since 2010], teaching college. It's... a perspective that I think is missing from Washington."
WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN KEY MIDTERM RACES SHOW

Pappas, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, highlighted that New Hampshire is "a state of voters who are pragmatic, who want their lives to be better and want problems to be solved, and I can demonstrate the ways that I've been working on those issues."

"It's expanding access to health care, building more affordable housing in New Hampshire, and ensuring that we're standing up to an administration that's ignoring the day-to-day concerns of Granite Staters," he added.
But Sununu wasn't the only one taking aim at Pappas as a do-nothing incumbent. Even his long-shot socialist rival in last week's primary took a shot.

First-time candidate and scientist Karishma Manzur, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, charged that "all [Pappas] wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C., go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is."
Pappas ended up crushing Manzur in the primary by a two-to-one margin, and Sununu defeated former Sen. Scott Brown in a landslide to capture the GOP nomination.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Democratic congressional candidate Karishma Manzur speaks to voters at a campaign stop in Dover, New Hampshire, on Sept. 3, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

With the general election sprint underway, Republican-aligned outside groups are now pouring millions into the state to target Pappas. And Pappas is using this week's Cook Political Report race rating to ring an alarm.
"MAGA super PACs are pouring millions of dollars a week into New Hampshire to try to flip this seat. And this race is officially a Toss Up," he warned on social media.
And Pappas told Fox News Digital recently that Sununu is "backed up by out-of-state special interests and dark money in this campaign. They're outspending us 3 to 1 on TV."
Firing back, this week a Democrat-aligned super PAC started running ads charging that, after he left the Senate, Sununu cashed in by working for lobbying firms.
Sununu was endorsed earlier this year by Trump, and since then Democrats have repeatedly tied the president, whose approval ratings are well into negative territory in New Hampshire, to Sununu.
Pappas called Sununu Trump's "hand-picked candidate."

Asked about the full-court press by Pappas and Democrats to anchor him to Trump, Sununu told Fox News Digital, "I've never even met the president."
But contrasting himself with Pappas, Sununu added that "there's no question I'll be a much more effective voice with this administration."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Leaked Trump plan sparks GOP showdown over how far Republicans should go to support families
summary: The Trump admin's $9,000 stay-at-home parent proposal sparks a fierce conservative divide, with some critics calling it socialism and a slippery slope.
story: Advancing American Freedom economist and welfare expert Rachel Greszler sounds alarm on possible stay-at-home parent program.

The Trump administration is reportedly floating a plan to let some married families with a stay-at-home parent tap federal childcare dollars — a proposal that has triggered a growing fight among conservatives over how far Washington should go to support family life.

The reported proposal would expand eligibility for Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) assistance to some married families in which one spouse works at least 35 hours a week and the other stays home, with the benefit averaging about $9,000 per child annually, according to reports.

The New York Times reported Sept. 5 that the administration was considering the proposal in the context of Vice President JD Vance’s long-standing advocacy for extending childcare assistance to stay-at-home parents, although a White House official told Fox News Digital that Vance has not pushed this specific proposal.
AMERICA’S CHILD CARE CRISIS NEEDS MORE PARENTAL FREEDOM — NOT MORE WASHINGTON CONTROL

Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance arrive for President Donald Trump to sign an executive order on foster children and families in the East Room of the White House, Nov. 13, 2025. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

"Until the administration officially unveils a policy push, any leaked reporting about potential policy ideas that have been neither fully baked nor released should be regarded as pointless speculation," said the official.

The Child Care and Development Block Grant was enacted in 1990 under President George H.W. Bush, and the 1996 welfare overhaul under President Bill Clinton amended the program and integrated it with mandatory childcare funding streams that are now commonly known as the Child Care and Development Fund.

In a White House press release posted close to Mother's Day, Trump touted how his administration is working to "better empower stay-at-home parents." In May, the Department of Health and Human Services issued new CCDF guidance clarifying states’ flexibility in how parents can choose among federally permitted childcare providers and services.

Critics of the reported proposal, including some Republican and conservative advocates, have warned that it could increase government oversight and create new concerns involving fraud, benefit cliffs, dependency or incentives around work.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene also labeled the idea as "socialism" in an X video, while conservative radio host Erick Erickson said on X the plan is "welfare for married people," and allegedly showed a recent pattern of the GOP pivoting toward "Diet Coke of Socialism."
TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME'
"I am old enough to remember a time when Republicans were against government entitlement programs," said Meghan McCain.

Some conservative figures and advocates have expressed support for the concept, arguing that federal policy should provide greater support to families that choose to have a parent remain home with children.

American Principles Project President Terry Schilling told Fox News Digital that the nuclear family needs to be reconsidered after years of government policies promoting multiple undergraduate and graduate degrees while delaying marriage and homeownership.

"For decades, Washington paid institutions to raise kids while lonely young people delayed marriage, homeownership and children," said Schilling. "If policy helped break the family, policy can help restore it to the center of American life by putting money in parents’ hands, not in the pockets of daycare chains, unions, and nonprofits."
The Advancing American Freedom (AAF) organization, founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, urged conservatives to oppose the reported plan.
Rachel Greszler, AAF economist and welfare expert, told Fox News Digital in an interview that "government is not the solution to family life."
"I fear that if we cross into that, that is taking what is supposed to be like a work-oriented welfare program and turning it into social engineering," she said.

Greszler expressed concern that sending government checks to stay-at-home parents would inevitably require guardrails to prevent fraud and abuse — potentially bringing greater government scrutiny into the home.
TRUMP’S WELFARE REFORMS ARE A MAJOR VICTORY. BUREAUCRATS COULD STILL WRECK THEM
Former Vice President Mike Pence following a Bloomberg Television interview in London, on Nov. 18, 2025. (Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"If we are going to invite checks for parents who are staying home with their children, you are also going to be inviting the government into your home to make sure that you are doing what they think you should be doing with a stay-at-home parent check," said Greszler.

She warned that even if conservatives are comfortable with how a Republican administration uses the program, establishing that government power could have unintended consequences if control of the White House changes hands.

"I worry that this would open the door into using taxpayer funds for social engineering. That in a different administration after another election could be used for the exact opposite intent of what certain conservatives are looking for right now to use it," Greszler added.
DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES

The proposal would reportedly disburse $9,000 per child, per year to pay "parent-based childcare" for married couples where one spouse works at least 35 hours a week and the other stays home. (Getty Images)

Schilling said the earlier Americans marry and start families, the more prosperous the country will be, and this program will give support to married families over commercial daycare networks to raise children.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Traditional welfare routes money through middlemen and too often subsidized family breakdown. This proposal works on the same principle as Republican healthcare reforms: instead of sending subsidies to insurance companies, put the money directly in the hands of families," he said.
Schilling says critics call it dependency when a parent stays home, but call it "investment" when a bureaucracy does it.

Florida GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna shared an article on the plan and wrote, "Being a stay-at-home parent is a full-time job and there should be resources and reward available to families that do this."
Fox News Digital reached out to the office of the vice president and the White House for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats reluctantly hand Trump major victory on fraud program targeting Tim Walz
summary: Hakeem Jeffries and over 140 House Democrats joined Republicans to make Trump's National Fraud Enforcement Division permanent in a 352-72 vote.
story: The Trump administration boosts efforts in its 'war on fraud,' including independent journalist Nick Shirley's Senate testimony exposing rampant tax dollar misuse.
President Donald Trump's crackdown on government fraud is getting unexpected backup from a majority of House Democrats, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.

More than 140 House Democrats voted with all Republicans to make the National Fraud Enforcement Division permanent on Wednesday. The bill passed in an overwhelming 352 to 72 vote, with all of its opponents being Democrats as well.

Trump's White House first announced the creation of a new division within the Department of Justice (DOJ) to combat fraud in January 2026, primarily targeting "fraud affecting the federal government, federally funded programs, and private citizens," according to a release by the administration.

It was notably used as a cudgel against Trump's political enemies earlier this year, when Vice President JD Vance referred Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and state Attorney General Keith Ellison to the fraud division for a potential criminal investigation.
WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

The House of Representatives passed a bill to codify President Donald Trump's fraud enforcement division in the Department of Justice. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Republicans accused Walz and Ellison of helping facilitate what's become a ballooning fraud scandal affecting Minnesota's social welfare programs. Both have acknowledged that taxpayer dollars were taken advantage of but accused GOP actors of casting the situation as worse than it actually is as a political attack.
VANCE REFERS TIM WALZ, MINNESOTA ATTORNEY GENERAL TO DOJ FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION OVER STATE'S ALLEGED FRAUD
The Trump administration's announcement of the fraud division also touted its actions in Minnesota, which it said was experiencing a "fraud epidemic."
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., a top House progressive, said he would give "tepid support" to the legislation, while pointing out a fraud division has already existed within the DOJ for decades.
REPUBLICANS DECLARE WAR ON 'ORGANIZED THEFT' WITH GOVERNMENT FRAUD CRACKDOWN

"This is hardly some kind of great breakthrough in law enforcement or criminal justice, but it is perhaps the least offensive piece of legislative flotsam and jetsam that has washed ashore in the last 48 hours of Republican chaos and retreat here in the House of Representatives," Raskin said on the House floor.
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz testifies during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., responded, "This conversation is about a piece of legislation. It's about a piece of legislation that we want to be enacted into law. It's not a partisan initiative. It's a permanent, nonpartisan commitment that we do something better because the people who are listening here... the people who are watching, they're getting tired of it."

"They're getting tired of all the money that has been wasted. And to try to pretend that just a few years ago, a couple of years ago, everything was perfect, everything was taken care of and that there was no corruption, we know better," Van Drew said.
Raskin spent a significant amount of time accusing Trump and his administration allies of corruption at the expense of prosecuting actual fraud cases, something Republicans pushed back against.

"What has come out of Minnesota over the last year, what has been exposed, is absolutely criminal in nature," said Rep. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyo. "I think what is coming, what is being exposed in blue cities and blue states run by Democrats, demonstrates that it's probably higher by an order of magnitude."
Raskin then targeted Van Drew directly in his comments: "My dear friend from New Jersey wants to make it sound like I'm doing something partisan. I'm joining his bill."
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., speaks during a House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Sept. 17, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It would be very easy for me to say I reject everything you do because you're on the side of this pro-fraud president, but I'm not doing that. Your bill says, let's call this the ‘National Fraud Enforcement Unit.’ I say, fine, that makes sense to me," Raskin said. "Why don't you cross the aisle and say it's wrong for them to be pardoning white-collar fraudster after white-collar fraudster, or at least pardoning them from having to pay the fines and the restitution back? It's an honest question. Do you really think that $1.7 billion should go from what was going to be the pockets of the victims back into the bank account of the perpetrators?"

Van Drew responded, "The gentleman has his numbers. He has his vision, he has his partisan ideas, and that's up to him. But I'm trying to point out today... we're trying to make something that is right now just an executive order and make it law to help the people."
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Republicans just got a powerful new playbook for the battle for Congress. Here's what's inside
summary: First on Fox: Advancing American Freedom unveils over 100 proposals to cut housing, energy and healthcare costs ahead of 2026 midterm elections.
story: Advancing American Freedom President Tim Chapman and Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at AAF, told Fox News Digital why they believe cutting regulations and expanding competition can lower costs.

FIRST ON FOX: With control of Congress on the line and pocketbook issues dominating the campaign trail, a prominent conservative group is unveiling a sweeping affordability agenda aimed at giving Republicans a sharper economic message ahead of the November midterm elections.

The Advancing American Freedom report, "Affordability 101," obtained first by Fox News Digital ahead of its Capitol Hill rollout Thursday, lays out more than 100 recommendations to lower the costs of housing, energy, food and healthcare by expanding supply, increasing competition and reducing government barriers.

The blueprint is a potential resource for Republican lawmakers and congressional staff while affordability emerges as one of the defining issues of the 2026 midterm elections. Founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, Advancing American Freedom argues costs can be lowered by reducing regulations, encouraging competition and boosting domestic production rather than creating new federal subsidies.

"We want free market conservative candidates to go out there and not just put on the red jersey or not just fight against the blue jersey, but to go there and give people ideas that actually work," Advancing American Freedom President Tim Chapman told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP’S AFFORDABILITY PLAN FACES CONSERVATIVE PUSHBACK AS POCKETBOOK ISSUES LOOM OVER MIDTERMS
President Donald Trump arrives on stage to deliver remarks on the economy at the Rocky Mount Event Center in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, on Dec. 19, 2025. (Daniel Torok/Official White House Photo)
Chapman argued the size and scope of government plays a larger role in affordability than many Americans realize.

"The size and scope of the government matters more than people understand in terms of its impact on the economy," Chapman said. "If you look at interest rates right now and how much of the skyrocketing interest rates are fueled by the debt and deficit problem, that's something we need to be concerned about as Americans."
Many of the proposals align with Trump administration priorities, including expanding domestic energy production, building more homes, reducing regulations and encouraging innovation.
But the blueprint also breaks with the administration on several issues.
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED
The blueprint argues that expanding domestic energy production and easing regulations on artificial intelligence and data centers can help lower costs. (Mark Wilson/Getty Images)

One flashpoint is Vice President JD Vance's proposal to expand childcare subsidies by broadening eligibility under the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), potentially providing some married families with a stay-at-home parent up to about $9,000 per child annually.

"His proposal sounds great, right?" Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "But the truth is, in many cases, it's a $9,000 divorce bonus."
On housing, the report says government regulations add 26.4% to the cost of a new single-family home and calls for permitting, zoning and land-use reforms to lower construction costs.
"I think those memos that deal with construction regulations and land use are the core group that would help affordability the most," Stern said.
5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS
The report is meant to give lawmakers concrete policy proposals they can take back to voters. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
The report also argues tariffs raise consumer prices, another point of disagreement with the administration.
"If you look at your grocery bill, how much of that is impacted by tariffs?" Chapman said. "That's driving up the price of goods and it's hurting people in their pocketbooks."

The blueprint also argues that expanding domestic energy production and easing regulations on artificial intelligence and data centers can help lower costs. Trump has championed rapid data center development despite growing concerns over electricity demand and local impacts.
"The counties that have data centers are making money off of it," Stern said. "They're actually reducing energy prices for those homes."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
As candidates sharpen their economic messages ahead of November, Chapman said the report is meant to give lawmakers concrete policy proposals they can take back to voters.

"We want people to have those solutions," Chapman said. "When they go home and talk to their constituents about the future of the country, they can say, 'I actually have an idea. Here's an idea for getting interest rates down or here's an idea for more small business growth.'"
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Brandon Johnson's latest viral moment sends Chicago critics into a frenzy: 'What the actual F?'
summary: Brandon Johnson's rooftop dance video sparked fierce backlash on X as critics highlight Chicago's 23% approval rating and rising crime stats.
story: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson joins a group dancing in a video that spread across X as he launched his reelection bid. (Credit: Instagram/ ravenreveals)
Social media is erupting over a viral video of Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson showing off his dance moves, with the clip quickly spreading across X as users call the performance "embarrassing."

The clip, circulating on X this week, shows Johnson dancing to "Hideaway" by Kiesza alongside a group on a rooftop, prompting conservative commentators to call out the mayor for seemingly neglecting the city’s crime problem.

Johnson’s campaign confirmed to Fox News Digital that he participated in the video but did not provide details about when it was filmed. The video circulated on X over the same weekend that Johnson announced Sunday that he would seek a second term.
PROGRESSIVE MINNEAPOLIS MAYOR'S VIRAL HIP-HOP MOVES SPARK 'HUMILIATION RITUAL' MOCKERY ONLINE
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks at a rally in Chicago on Oct. 18, 2025. (Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images)
"What the actual F?," asked Fox News contributor Joe Concha.
"1,320 people shot in Chicago in 2026 so far," wrote popular X account End Wokeness, sharing the video.
"Chicago does not need another influencer with a title," wrote popular X account True Patriot Voice.
"23% approval rating. 40 people shot per week. Thugs doing ‘street takeovers’ every week. Businesses fleeing," said conservative commentator Benny Johnson.
"Pathetic," said New York Post contributor Miranda Devine.
BRANDON JOHNSON BLASTED BY FELLOW DEMOCRAT AFTER TEEN ALLEGEDLY STRIKES 5 OFFICERS DURING TAKEOVER CHAOS

Mayor of Chicago Brandon Johnson testifies during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing with sanctuary city mayors, at the U.S. Capitol, on Wednesday, March 5, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Graeme Sloan for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
"Embarrassing and pathetic," said another user.
"Brandon Johnson should be impeached for making this video," said Ambassador Nick Adams, special presidential envoy for American tourism, exceptionalism and values.
"Keep voting failures in Chicagoans," said Kaltbaum Capital President Gary Kaltbaum.
TRUMP TAKES AIM AT POPE LEO XIV MEETING WITH 'USELESS' CHICAGO MAYOR BRANDON JOHNSON AT VATICAN
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks during a press conference on the fifth floor of City Hall on Jan. 27, 2026, in Chicago. (Chris Sweda / Chicago Tribune)
Johnson was first elected as the Windy City’s mayor in 2023 and announced he will be seeking a second term over the weekend.

Chicago has long struggled with crime, and Chicago Police Department data through June 26 showed shootings up about 3% from the same period last year and motor-vehicle thefts up 10%. Preliminary Cook County Medical Examiner data showed 219 homicides through June 30, compared with 208 during the first half of 2025.
