Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
Virginia's warning after a call she thought she could trust
Virginia wrote to CyberGuy after the experience because she wanted other people to know how quickly a seemingly safe phone call can go wrong.

"Hi, I just wanted to pass on this scam. I needed to call American Express. Instead of using the phone number on my credit card, I asked Siri to call American Express instead. It was all downhill from that point on. The telephone number was bogus, and eventually I wound up on my BOA account with a so-called BOA Security Expert. Fortunately, when zeros started being added to the $1000.00 credit I was supposed to get, and the "gentleman" said he couldn't correct it, I needed to go to BOA and return the $100000.00. I realized what was going on and immediately hung up and froze my BOA account. I never expected that a number that Siri provided would lead to trouble. I try to inform people now that calling a number can also put your finances in jeopardy. I am 82 years old and could have lost my entire retirement in one fell swoop. Thank you," Virginia, Concord, Massachusetts.

That last part stopped me. Virginia had no reason to think asking Siri to place a call could potentially put her retirement savings in danger. After all, she initiated the call herself. That gave the person who answered an immediate advantage.
How Virginia's Siri bank scam appears to have worked

Based on Virginia's account, this looks like two scam techniques chained together. First came the fake customer service number. Then came a refund or overpayment scheme designed to persuade her to send real money back.

Virginia says she asked Siri to call American Express rather than using the phone number printed on her card. Apple says business information can appear across Apple services, including Maps and Siri. Place cards can include phone numbers and other business details.

We reached out to Apple for comment but did not hear back before our deadline. However, Virginia's experience alone cannot tell us how this specific bogus number became associated with her request. We simply do not know how the bad number got there.

This was a powerful setup because Virginia believed she had contacted American Express herself. She had not answered a random phone call. She had asked her iPhone to make the call. That can lower your guard before the person on the other end even says hello.

The Better Business Bureau has warned about this problem. Scammers can promote fake support numbers that make their way into online search results. Voice assistants may then use information pulled from those results or related business listings.

We have seen a similar trap with traditional web searches. In our report, The No. 1 Google search scam everyone falls for, a victim searching for customer support landed on a fake number and eventually lost control of his phone. Voice assistants can add another layer of trust because you may never see the number before the call starts.

According to Virginia, she eventually found herself dealing with someone claiming to be a Bank of America security expert. At that point, the story had shifted from customer service to her bank account. That shift should immediately raise your guard. Bank of America warns about criminals who pose as bank representatives and invent urgent problems involving your account. Scammers may ask for verification codes, remote access or money transfers. Then Virginia encountered the clue that saved her.

Virginia says she expected a $1,000 credit. Then zeros started appearing. Suddenly, she was dealing with $100,000. The supposed bank expert told her the mistake could not be corrected. According to Virginia, she was then told she needed to go to Bank of America and return the excess money. That follows a familiar overpayment or refund scam pattern.

Scammers claim they accidentally sent too much money. Then they pressure you to return the difference before you have time to verify what happened. Fortunately, the sudden jump to $100,000 made Virginia question the entire story. She hung up and froze her Bank of America account.

We cannot determine that from Virginia's description. Scammers sometimes use remote-access software to manipulate what a person sees on a computer. They can also move a victim's own money between accounts, so it appears that a new deposit arrived. Another possibility involves a fake banking page designed to display whatever balance the criminal wants the victim to see.

CyberGuy has covered how fake support representatives use remote access and other tactics to take control of devices. You can see the warning signs in our guide, Protect yourself from tech support scams. Virginia did not provide enough information to identify the exact technique used here.

What we do know is that the criminal wanted her to believe $100,000 had appeared and that she needed to return it. If she had followed those instructions, the money she sent would have been very real.
NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS
Before calling your bank or credit card company, experts recommend verifying the phone number through your card or official banking app. (Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Ways to protect yourself from fake customer service calls
A scammer may know your name, your bank or details that make the call sound convincing. These steps can help you stay in control.

For banks and credit card companies, the safest starting point is usually the number printed on the back of your physical card. You can also open the institution's official app and find its contact information there. Avoid relying on a phone number supplied by a search result, sponsored ad or voice assistant when your finances are involved.

A call to your credit card company should not suddenly require you to move money through an unrelated bank account. If the story starts getting complicated, hang up. Then contact the company again using a verified number.

A scammer may claim your money needs to be transferred into another account to keep it safe. Do not do it. Bank of America warns that it will never ask customers to transfer money because fraud was detected on an account. The same caution applies if someone tells you to withdraw cash, buy gift cards or purchase cryptocurrency to resolve a banking problem.

If someone says $1,000 accidentally became $100,000, stop. Do not transfer the supposed difference back. Contact your bank independently and ask it to verify your actual balance and transaction history.

Banks use one-time codes to confirm your identity or approve certain actions. A scammer may ask you to read one aloud while claiming it is needed to cancel fraud. Never give a verification code to someone who called you or someone you reached through an unverified number.

If someone claiming to represent a bank or credit card company tells you to install software that lets them see or control your screen, end the call. Remote-access programs can give criminals enormous control over your computer. They may watch you log into your bank, move money between accounts or manipulate what appears on the screen.

Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a fake support representative sends you to a malicious website or convinces you to download a dangerous file. It can also warn you about phishing pages and other threats designed to steal passwords or financial information. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, keeping your personal information and digital assets safe. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Set alerts for purchases, withdrawals and transfers so you know quickly when money moves. You should also enable notifications for suspicious logins and changes to your account information when your financial institution offers them. These alerts give you another chance to catch activity you did not authorize.

Your banking password should never be reused on another account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Also enable two-factor authentication whenever your bank supports it. An authenticator app or security key can provide stronger protection when available.

If someone tells you money suddenly appeared in your account, do not rely on what they show you. Close the session. Open your bank's official app yourself or type the bank's website address directly into your browser. Then check your transactions independently.

If Siri or Apple Maps provides incorrect business information, you can report the listing to Apple. On an iPhone, open Maps > tap your picture or initials next to the search field > tap Reports > tap Report a New Issue > choose the appropriate option and follow the on-screen instructions. Fixing a bad listing may help prevent someone else from reaching the same number.
APPLE’S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: ARE YOU OWED CASH?
A Massachusetts woman froze her bank account after spotting red flags in what appeared to be a refund scam that began with a Siri phone call. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What to do if you already gave a scammer access
If you think a scammer got access to your financial information, act quickly.
Hang up and stop responding to texts, emails or calls from the person. Do not use a callback number they provided.
Use the number on your card or inside the official app. Tell the fraud department exactly what happened. Ask whether any transfers, new payees or other account changes need to be stopped.
Virginia froze her Bank of America account as soon as she realized something was wrong. Your bank may also allow you to lock a debit or credit card instantly through its app.
If you entered a password while the scammer could see your screen, or you gave one away, change it from a trusted device. Change any other account that used the same or a similar password.

If you installed a remote-control program at the scammer's direction, disconnect that computer from the internet. Remove the software and run a full antivirus scan before signing back into sensitive accounts. If you are unsure whether the device is clean, get help from a trusted computer professional before using it for banking again.
Look for unfamiliar transactions, new payees and changes to your phone number or email address. Also check whether the scammer altered security settings or added a new device to the account.

If the scammer obtained your Social Security number or enough personal information to open accounts in your name, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open new credit in your name.

Report financial fraud to your bank immediately. You can also file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If money was transferred, contact the financial institution involved as soon as possible. Some transactions become much harder to recover once they are completed.

Criminals may contact victims again after the first attempt. Sometimes they pretend to be investigators, bank employees or recovery specialists who claim they can get your money back. Treat any unexpected follow-up contact with suspicion.
Kurt's key takeaways

What sticks with me about Virginia's story is how ordinary the first move felt. She was trying to reach a company she already trusted and used Siri to save herself a little time. That tiny convenience nearly opened the door to a six-figure loss. Virginia also deserves credit for catching the moment when the story stopped making sense. A $1,000 credit becoming $100,000 was enough to make her question the person guiding her.

That instinct protected her retirement. I also would not frame this as an age issue. Criminals succeed because they exploit trust in familiar technology and recognizable financial brands. Anyone can get caught when a call begins through a device they use every day. From now on, I would treat financial phone numbers almost like passwords. Verify them before you use them. The number on your physical card or inside the official banking app gives you a much stronger starting point than a search result or voice request.

After hearing what happened to Virginia, would you still let Siri dial your bank without checking the number first? Have you ever reached the wrong company through a voice assistant or online search? Write to us in the comments below and tell us what happened. Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: Researcher delivers extinction warning
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon discusses his resignation from the company and concerns over artificial intelligence safety on ‘Special Report.’
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- Researcher who departed AI role over fears of racing into extinction says people are 'begging' for regulation
- 9/11 hero’s legacy lives on 25 years later as son unveils new tech lifeline for those facing grief
- Nobody wants AI-generated sports commentators, but a pro golf tournament is introducing one anyway

'GAMBLE': The Anthropic researcher who is leaving the company over fears the technology is gambling with human life told Fox News there is hope that we can avoid the chance it could destroy humankind within the next decade.

BEYOND THE PAIN: A father's legacy is living on through a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool that helps others navigate grief and trauma — two-and-a-half decades after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

SMART FLEX: Apple on Wednesday unveiled a highly anticipated foldable version of the iPhone along with other consumer tech devices embedded with artificial intelligence in the first major product event under the leadership of new CEO John Ternus.
Apple CEO John Ternus displays the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)
NEXT-GEN SIDEKICK: Meta on Tuesday rolled out a long-planned personal artificial intelligence agent aimed at helping users complete daily tasks.

THREAT ALERT: Anthropic said Thursday it disrupted several attempts this year by researchers to use its AI models for biological research that could potentially aid the development of biological weapons, prompting the company to ban accounts and strengthen its safeguards.

RACE TO NOWHERE: Golf fans who tune into this week's New Mexico Open broadcast will be introduced to a new commentator by the name of Duff Foreman. He'll join former PGA Tour winner Notah Begay III and well-known broadcaster Ryan Burr on the call, although Foreman won't technically be on site, seeing as how he's not an actual person.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, accompanied by President Donald Trump, Oracle co-founder, CTO and Executive Chairman Larry Ellison and SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son speaks during a news conference in the Roosevelt Room of the White House on Jan. 21, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

SILICON HANDSHAKE: The federal government under President Donald Trump reached an agreement with OpenAI on a landmark deal to equip government employees with the most cutting-edge artificial intelligence models at a major discount, Fox News Digital has learned.

'SEAT AT THE TABLE': A GOP insider making the conservative case for regulating artificial intelligence development predicts President Donald Trump's full-throated support for data center expansion will soon change after he hears from the American people on the midterm campaign trail.

THE NEW GOLD RUSH: As Americans weigh the costs and benefits of massive data centers emerging in their towns to fuel the artificial intelligence boom, the country's reddest state could be poised to capitalize on billions of dollars in investment that other states are increasingly reluctant to welcome.

An Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia, US, on Sunday, July 28, 2024. Data center developers in Northern Virginia are asking utility Dominion Energy Inc. for as much power as several nuclear reactors can generate, in the latest sign of how artificial intelligence is helping drive up electricity demand. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)

CUT OF THE DEAL: As opposition to artificial intelligence data centers spreads across rural America, one group is proposing "data center dividends" to counter the backlash by allowing residents to share directly in the wealth generated by the technology hubs.
BOLD FRONTIER: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang declared that the era of artificial general intelligence (AGI) has arrived after OpenAI released its latest model.

AISLE BE WATCHING: Artificial intelligence is making its way into the grocery aisle, and it could have an unexpected effect on how much you spend. You grab a grocery cart, start working through your list and notice a screen on the handle offering directions, coupons and product suggestions. It can keep a running total and may even let you skip the checkout line. That sounds convenient. It also gives the store a new way to reach you while you are deciding what goes into your cart.

title: 8 biggest things we learned from Apple's 2026 event
summary: iPhone Duo opens to a 7.6-inch foldable display starting at $1,999, but Siri Recap's ambient listening on Apple Watch may spark privacy concerns.
story: Apple's newly unveiled foldable iPhone Duo sparks significant consumer interest despite a hefty $1,999 starting price tag. On 'Varney & Co.', Taylor Riggs explains the premium device's unique dual-screen capability and ultra-thin design. Host Stuart Varney admits he plans to purchase the high-end smartphone, which can cost up to $3,000 for the two-terabyte storage model.
Apple finally did it. After years of watching Samsung, Google and other phone makers experiment with foldables, Apple has entered the race with iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone.

It's the announcement everyone is talking about, but it was hardly the only thing that stood out. Apple also showed us an iPhone camera that can help prove a photo is authentic. Siri AI is getting far more personal. Apple Watch will soon be able to summarize conversations you want to remember. Even AirPods are getting smarter at a lower starting price.

Some of these upgrades feel genuinely useful. Others raise questions about privacy, price and how much intelligence we want built into the devices around us. So, after sorting through everything Apple announced, here are the eight biggest things we learned from Apple's 2026 event and what they could mean for you.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
IS APPLE INTELLIGENCE ON YOUR IPHONE REALLY SECURE?

From foldable phones to AI-powered wearables, Apple's latest announcements signal a push toward more intelligent everyday devices. (Apple)
1) iPhone Duo is Apple's big foldable swing

Let's start with the product everyone is talking about. iPhone Duo opens to a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display. Apple says that gives you 50% more screen area than iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 5.4-inch outer display offers 90% of the screen area of iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple also tackled one of the biggest complaints about foldables: the crease. The company developed a custom nano-texture finish that reduces glare and reflections. Apple says the finish also minimizes the visibility of the crease while giving the display a matte feel.

There are some other unexpected choices. Instead of Face ID, iPhone Duo uses Touch ID built into the side button. You can enroll multiple fingers, so unlocking works in different positions. Apple Pencil with USB-C support will arrive later this year. The phone uses Grade 5 titanium. Apple also says it carries an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance.

The folding design also creates some camera tricks you can't get on a regular iPhone. Dual Capture can show your front and rear camera feeds at the same time during FaceTime, while Duo FaceTime lets someone beside you join the call using the outer display. You can also use that outer screen to frame higher-quality selfies with the rear cameras.

Apple added a few other clever touches. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see the shot before you take it, while Kid Cue uses animations to get a child's attention. Smart Take can even watch the scene and automatically snap a photo when everyone is ready. Then comes the part that may give you sticker shock: the price. iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage. Apple will offer configurations up to 2TB. Preorders begin Oct. 16, with availability starting Oct. 23.
2) Apple redesigned iOS around the fold

The hardware grabs your eye, but the software could decide whether Duo succeeds. Apple changed iOS 27 so content moves between the outside and inside displays. Open the phone and apps can expand onto the larger screen.
You can also put two apps side by side. Mail can show your inbox alongside a message. The Home Screen can display two pages at once. The system also responds when you fold or rotate the phone.

That caught my attention because a folding screen needs to earn its extra cost. If I open a phone this large, I want more than a bigger version of the same app. Apple is also giving developers tools to take advantage of the design. During the event, Apple showed Zoom using the expanded screen for video calls and Netflix adapting its experience to the two displays.

The cameras use the second screen too. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outer display. Meanwhile, Smart Take can follow a scene and automatically snap the photo when everyone looks ready. Those are the features that could make the folding design useful after the initial wow factor wears off.
Apple CEO John Ternus displays the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)
3) iPhone 18 Pro gets much more serious about photography

If a foldable phone doesn't interest you, Apple gave the regular Pro lineup a substantial camera upgrade. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max use a 48MP Fusion Main camera with a variable aperture.

The camera can automatically adjust the aperture depending on lighting and depth of field. Apple also gives photographers manual control through four aperture settings: ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4.0.
In darker environments, opening the aperture lets in more light. A narrower aperture can keep more of a scene in focus. However, another camera feature may prove even more important.

Apple Reference Image securely signs photo data at the pixel level when the picture is captured. Apple says that can help verify exactly what the camera sensor saw. Think about where we're headed with AI-generated images.

Being able to verify that an image began as an actual camera capture could become valuable for journalists, investigators or anyone documenting something important. That feature may get less attention than the new camera hardware. I wouldn't overlook it.
iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. Preorders begin Sept. 12, with both phones available starting Sept. 18.
APPLE RAISES PRICES AS AI CHIP COSTS SURGE
4) Battery life may be the iPhone 18 Pro upgrade you feel most

Apple can show us faster chips every year. Most of us notice battery life much faster. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max can deliver up to 45 hours of video playback, the longest battery life the company has offered in an iPhone. It also rates the Pro Max for up to 30 hours of general use per charge.
Charging gets faster too. Apple says iPhone 18 Pro can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes with a compatible adapter. Underneath it all sits the A20 Pro chip.

Apple built A20 Pro using 2-nanometer technology. The chip includes a second Neural Engine, bringing the total to 32 Neural Engine cores. Apple says that doubles compute power for advanced on-device models. The new Pro models also use a redesigned vapor chamber to manage heat. Faster performance sounds good. More time away from a charger is something you'll notice every day.
5) Siri AI is moving from keynote promise to everyday use

Siri AI had a big role in Apple's Sept. 9 iPhone 18 Pro unveiling. Apple showed how its rebuilt assistant can use your personal context, understand what you're looking at and take action across the apps you already use.

During the event, Apple showed someone asking what her mother wanted to cook during an upcoming visit. Siri searched Mail and Messages to find the answer. Apple also demonstrated Siri working through the Camera app. Point your iPhone at something and Siri can answer questions about what you're seeing or take action based on what's around you.

There's also a new Siri app on the Home Screen. You can use it to start a conversation or return to an earlier one, with conversations syncing privately through iCloud. Siri AI begins rolling out in beta in English on Sept. 14 with iOS 27. Apple says support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish will follow in October.
Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during an announcement of new products on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)
6) Siri Recap may start a big privacy conversation

This one made me pay attention. Apple announced Siri Recap for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It uses ambient listening to turn conversations into high-level notes. Apple says each recap can include a title, summary and key points that appear in the Siri app. You control where and when Siri Recap takes notes. For example, you could allow it at work but disable it at night.

Then there is Live Rewind. Double-click the Digital Crown and Apple Watch can transcribe what was said during the previous 15 seconds. You can then review what you missed. That's useful if you missed something someone said in a noisy restaurant. Naturally, ambient listening raises privacy questions.

Apple says these Audio Intelligence features do not create or store audio recordings. The company says raw audio used for processing remains inaccessible, even to Apple. Apple also says Audio Intelligence does not identify or attribute speakers. Live Rewind transcripts and Siri Recaps use end-to-end encryption when syncing through iCloud.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind require Siri AI. Apple says both will arrive in beta later this year, starting in English. I like the idea of getting help remembering an important conversation. However, I would want to know exactly when the feature is active every time I use it.
7) Apple Watch gets smarter about your health

Apple Watch is becoming more aggressive about turning health data into something you can understand. Series 12 and Ultra 4 use Apple's new Health Sensing System. According to Apple, Apple Watch Series 12 can now measure heart rate every five seconds throughout the day. Apple also says heart rate variability is measured up to 24 times more often than before. Apple says its head-to-head testing found the system delivered the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.

For everyday users, Readiness may be the more relatable feature. Each morning, Apple Watch analyzes your recent activity, sleep and vital signs. It then gives you a score designed to help you decide whether to push harder or recover. The score can also change during the day.

Meanwhile, Apple Watch Ultra 4 gets up to 50 hours of normal use. Max Extended Workout mode can reach 45 hours. Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. Both are available to preorder now and will be available starting Sept. 18.

Apple also showed how the iPhone and Apple Watch can work together to assess how your body is moving. With Movement Evaluations in the redesigned Health app, you can position your iPhone so the camera can see you, then follow guided exercises while vision-based AI analyzes your movements.

Apple says the assessments can look at flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics and VO2 max. They can also help you track your progress while recovering from an injury. Apple says the processing happens on your device, and no video is recorded, stored or shared.
SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 LINEUP ADDS THREE CHOICES

Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during the keynote address at Apple’s "Surprise and Shine" event at the company's corporate headquarters, Apple Park, on September 9, 2026, in Cupertino, California. The event featured Apple product announcements and was Apple CEO John Ternus’s first keynote address in his new role. (Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)
8) AirPods 5 could be one of the event's better values

The final surprise may appeal to people who have no interest in spending $1,999 on a foldable phone. Apple announced AirPods 5 with Active Noise Cancellation for $129. Apple says the new earbuds provide stronger Active Noise Cancellation than the previous generation. They keep an open-ear design for people who prefer not to use silicone ear tips. The standard $129 model gets up to four hours of listening with ANC enabled. The charging case brings the total to up to 20 hours.

A $149 version adds volume swipe on the stem and a wireless charging case. It gets up to five hours per charge with ANC and up to 22 hours with the case and ANC enabled. Both versions are available starting Sept. 18, with preorders open now.
AirPods 5 also support Live Translation and Siri AI. During the event, Apple showed AirPods translating Spanish into English while the wearer continued a face-to-face conversation.
Compared with iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 may seem like a smaller announcement. Still, the $129 model could end up being one of the products far more people actually buy.
Kurt's key takeaways

Apple gave us plenty to talk about, but iPhone Duo is the one people are going to want to pick up and play with. I certainly do. At $1,999, it carries a premium price, but Apple is clearly betting that the larger screen and new foldable experiences will be enough to tempt early adopters. What interests me more is how much smarter these devices are becoming. Siri AI finally looks like it could understand enough about your day to be genuinely helpful. Siri Recap sounds incredibly convenient too, but a watch that can summarize conversations around you deserves some healthy scrutiny about when it's listening and how clearly you know it's active. Then there are improvements you don't need a demo to appreciate. Give me longer iPhone battery life any day. And Apple Reference Image could become far more important than it sounds today if we reach a point where you can no longer trust your eyes to tell whether a photo is real.
After everything Apple announced, what would actually convince you to upgrade, and what would make you hold onto the device you already have? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Philadelphia home search uncovers possible human ashes, images of 7 missing women: police
summary: Ashtrays containing possible human remains and images of seven missing women were found among over 1 million files inside Eugene Horsch's Philadelphia home.
story: Police in Philadelphia gave an update on a case after a search of Eugene Horsch's home led to the discovery of over 1 million images, some containing depictions of missing women appearing unconscious. Credit: FOX 29 Philadelphia

Philadelphia police found images of seven missing women, including two who appear unconscious and injured, while searching more than 1 million images recovered from a home where investigators also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said Wednesday.

Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Armando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said during a news conference.
Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017.
CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS
"Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said. "To date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."
The home belonged to deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch and was occupied by his son, Eugene Horsch, whose June arrest sparked the investigation.
R.C. Horsch in a 1999 mugshot. (S. E. Stokowski/Wikimedia Creative Commons)
On June 19, a Federal Park Ranger arrested Eugene Horsch, 44, after investigating him and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained.

"During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said.

The female passenger presented police with a false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital.
FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY
A photo of Blair Tonzelli, who went missing in February 2023. (National Missing and Unidentified Persons System)
The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown.

After obtaining a warrant, investigators found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras and phones," Vanore said during the press conference.

Investigators have identified 58 people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them."
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS
Eugene Horsch's mugshot (FOX 29 Philadelphia)
One video shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Police identified this woman as Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia.
Another missing woman connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported.
Two other missing women have been connected to the home. Police identified one as a 25-year-old woman but did not name her, and the other has yet to be identified, according to FOX 29.
Maribel Fresses, who went missing in 2018. (National Missing and Unidentified Persons System)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We have only processed a small fraction of the total media. Thousands of videos remain to be analyzed. We are working to corroborate what we see and gather physical evidence to prove our findings, supported throughout by the FBI as we determine our next steps," Vanore concluded Wednesday.

title: Body of missing hiker found in Olympic National Park thanks to crucial clue
summary: Neil Gehring left Olympic National Park's Madison Falls Trailhead for an overnight trek and never returned.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The body of a missing 26-year-old hiker in Washington state's Olympic National Park was recovered nearly two weeks after he set out on a backcountry trek, following a crucial break in the search, officials said.
Searchers located Neil Gehring on the northwest slope of Mount Appleton after receiving and analyzing additional cellphone location data, according to the National Park Service.
Search-and-rescue teams recovered Gehring’s body Sunday evening. He was taken to the Clallam County Coroner’s Office at about 8 p.m. on Sept. 13.
MISSING 70-YEAR-OLD HIKER RESCUED AFTER DISAPPEARING FOR A WEEK IN REMOTE NATIONAL PARK

Neil Gehring, 26, set out on the Madison Falls Trailhead in Olympic National Park on Aug. 31 and was due to return on Sept. 1. But he failed to return and was reported overdue on Sept. 2. Search teams recovered his body on Sept. 13. (National Park Service)
Officials did not release details about the cellphone data or the circumstances of Gehring’s death.
Gehring left the Madison Falls Trailhead on Aug. 31 for what was supposed to be an overnight backcountry trip.
His permit showed that he planned to make a cross-country trek from Boulder Lake to Appleton Pass before returning to the trailhead on Sept. 1.
Gehring was reported overdue at 6:30 a.m. the next morning, prompting an immediate search.
Searchers located Gehring after receiving and analyzing additional cellphone location data. NPS did not immediately provide details about the data or a cause of death. (National Park Service)
MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE
For the next 10 days, teams searched his expected route from the air and ground, using drones and dogs as part of the effort.
By Sept. 11, the park announced it was changing tactics after the searches failed to locate Gehring. Teams would instead focus on finding new clues that could help narrow the search.
Investigators also asked anyone who had been in the area or had information about Gehring’s whereabouts to come forward.
Two days later, searchers found Gehring after receiving and analyzing the additional cellphone location data.
Gehring's body was recovered from the northwest slope of Mount Appleton on Sept. 13, officials said. (NPS/Pablo McLoud)
Olympic National Park thanked the search-and-rescue teams that volunteered to help with the effort.

NPS said no additional information was available at this time.

title: Husband stands by wife accused of killing son, plotting to poison him after Clancy trial obsession: attorney
summary: Corie Walsh allegedly claimed her 2-year-old son Barrett was the "devil" during a psychotic episode. Prosecutors allege she also plotted to poison her husband.
story: Eugene Roy, former Chicago Police Chief of Detectives, tells Fox News Digital that a psychiatric defense in a child murder case like Corie Walsh's is "very rare" and "more predominant in adult cases."

The husband of an Illinois mother accused of strangling their 2-year-old son during a "psychotic episode" is standing by her, even as prosecutors say she also plotted to poison him amid a fixation with the Lindsay Clancy trial, according to her attorney.

Corie Walsh, 38, told officers that she killed her 2-year-old son Barrett on Sept. 1 because she believed he was the "devil" and "Antichrist," according to documents obtained by Fox News Digital. He was found hanging in the basement from a rafter, officials said.

A neighbor found the toddler and administered CPR while calling 911, with court documents noting he was "cold and had no pulse." The 2-year-old was pronounced dead later that day at New Lenox Hospital. Barrett's cause of death was determined to be "asphyxia due to ligature compression of the neck." Walsh was treated at a local hospital for self-inflicted wounds to her wrists and thighs.
Defense attorneys for Walsh said her husband and mother "have unwavering love and support" for her.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Corie A. Walsh, 38, in a booking photo provided by law enforcement. Prosecutors are asking a judge to deny her pretrial release following the death of her 2-year-old son. (Will County Detention Facility)
Walsh's husband and mother weren't at her detention hearing on Sept. 8 because that was the same day as Barrett's funeral.
Andrea Lyon, a defense attorney for Walsh who previously served on Casey Anthony's defense team, told Fox News Digital in a statement that Walsh's actions were driven by mental illness.

"This is a tragedy for the Walsh family, all of whom are mourning the loss of this child," Lyon said. "It is also a tragedy in that Corie herself was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time this happened."

Lyon acknowledged that Walsh was "psychotic" but denied that her client's interest in the Clancy case had any connection to the alleged killing.

"They are not correlated at all. It's just accidental," Lyon said, describing as "baseless and cruel" any suggestion that Walsh's actions constituted a copycat crime.

Corie Walsh, right, poses with her husband and children inside a church. Walsh faces three counts of first-degree murder in the death of her 2-year-old son, Barrett. (CREDIT: Facebook/ Corie Walsh)

Court documents indicate that Walsh had "recently become very invested" in the murder trial for Clancy, who was accused of murdering her three children. Clancy acknowledged she killed her children but argued she was experiencing postpartum psychosis.

Walsh "had been actively discussing the [Clancy] case via group text message with her friends up until 12:30 PM on September 1, 2026, three and a half hours before the scene was discovered."

Police tape surrounds the Frankfort, Illinois, home where officers found an unresponsive 2-year-old boy. (Fox 32 Chicago)
LINDSAY CLANCY FIXATION AND ALLEGED PLOT TO POISON HUSBAND EMERGE AS ACCUSED MOM CLAIMS PSYCHOSIS

Retired Chicago Police Chief of Detectives Eugene Roy told Fox News Digital that a psychiatric defense rarely succeeds in cases like this one, and is more common in adult cases than those involving children.

"It's very rare. It's more predominant in adult cases," Roy said. "Cases like this are, with children involved, because of the publicity and just the pain it causes the community are what we call heaters. There's a lot of media focus on them. There's a lot of attention. There's a lot of demands to resolve the case promptly."

title: Idaho prosecutors accuse Bryan Kohberger of 'fishing' to find better arguments for bid to withdraw guilty plea
summary: Bryan Kohberger's new legal team seeks more time for post-conviction relief, but Idaho prosecutors call the discovery request a "fishing expedition."
story: Legal maneuvers escalate in the Idaho student murders case as Bryan Kohberger attempts to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler. Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett breaks down the defense's strategy.
Idaho prosecutors are accusing Bryan Kohberger's new legal team of attempting a "fishing expedition" and trying to buy time to find better arguments for his bid to withdraw his guilty plea.

"Unfortunately for [Kohberger], that is not how discovery in post-conviction proceedings works," Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote in a response to the convicted killer's request for more time to file an amended petition.
The deadline is currently set for Nov. 13 — four years to the day since the Idaho student murders in Moscow.
BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

Kohberger's lawyers argue that the deadline would force them to irrevocably waive any claims not included in the amended petition, which is due before discovery deadlines set for next year. They want to see discovery materials before filing it.
Read Kohberger's request for more time:

"Post-conviction discovery is supposed to assist you and your lawyers in proving a legitimate constitutional claim, in this case, ineffective assistance of counsel," said Randolph Rice, a Maryland-based attorney and legal analyst who has been following the case.

Madison Mogen, top left, smiles on the shoulders of her best friend, Kaylee Goncalves, as they pose with Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and two other housemates in Goncalves' final Instagram post, shared the day before the four students were stabbed to death. (@kayleegoncalves/Instagram)
"It isn't supposed to be a fishing expedition to help you invent a new one," he added. "You don't get to throw a fishing net into the discovery ocean and hope you pull up a constitutional violation."

title: San Diego bystanders chase down suspected Tesla thief after woman struck on boardwalk
summary: Video captured on smart glasses shows bystander Alex Srour chasing down a suspect who allegedly drove a stolen Tesla through a San Diego pedestrian walkway.
story: A group of good Samaritans in San Diego chased down a suspected car thief who allegedly barreled through a pedestrian walkway, injuring at least one person. Credit: Storyful / @alexhsrour via Storyful

Bystanders chased down and tackled a suspected car thief after he allegedly drove a stolen Tesla through a crowded San Diego pedestrian walkway, striking a woman and leaving her with serious injuries.
Video shows Juan Antonio Gonzaba, 39, fleeing the vehicle, which police told numerous local media outlets was stolen, and sprinting through a parking lot.
Bystander Alex Srour leaped into action, chasing Gonzaba down and pushing him while he ran, resulting in Gonzaba falling to the ground.

"I hear somebody behind me just scream like, ‘Watch out.’ And then I look and there's like a Tesla just barreling at me going like 70 miles an hour," Srour told KABC-TV.
Juan Antonio Gonzaba flees after driving an allegedly stolen Tesla through a pedestrian walkway (Storyful / @alexhsrour via Storyful)
Police charged Gonzaba with assault with a deadly weapon, hit-and-run and auto theft in connection with the incident, according to the San Diego Sheriff's Office.

Srour, who recorded the incident on a pair of smart glasses he was wearing, said he was sideswiped when Gonzaba careened the Tesla down a pedestrian boardwalk.
The Tesla that Juan Antonio Gonzaba allegedly stole and drove through a pedestrian boardwalk in San Diego is seen in aerial footage. (Storyful / @alexhsrour via Storyful)
"He hit my bike, and it like pushed me really, it like launched me off to the side," Srour told KABC, adding, "People don't expect a car to come through the boardwalk like it's just not normal."

Gonzaba allegedly struck a 25-year-old woman, who was transferred to the hospital with injuries that included a fractured spine, broken ribs and a cut that required 20 stitches, prosecutors told KNSD-TV.
Gonzaba is being held without bail in the San Diego Central Jail after prosecutors noted that he has an extensive criminal history, KNSD reported.

The scene unfolded Wednesday along State Route 238, about 20 miles west of Maricopa, where the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office reported two people in their 80s stuck inside a vehicle, according to AZ Family.

"Reminder, crossing flooded roadways can have dangerous and many times deadly outcomes," the Sheriff’s Office posted to Facebook along with a video showing a helicopter arriving at the scene. title: Texas man who killed 3 in 2005 burglary executed after warden asks him for last words
summary: LeJames Norman was the fifth death row inmate executed in Texas this year after he pleaded guilty to capital murder in a 2005 triple killing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Texas death row inmate was given one final opportunity to speak Wednesday evening, moments before the state executed him for the murders of three people during a botched 2005 robbery.
LeJames Norman, 40, had nothing to say.
When the warden asked whether he wanted to make a final statement, Norman simply shook his head before he was put to death by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville.
ARIZONA EXECUTES MAN WHO KILLED VICTIM BY DOUSING HIM IN GASOLINE AND SETTING HIM ON FIRE IN 2002 ATTACK
This photo provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows LeJames Norman on Feb. 28, 2024. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
Norman was sentenced to death for fatally shooting Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, inside the Edna home they shared, about 100 miles southwest of Houston.
According to court records, Norman and Ker’Sean Ramey believed there was cocaine inside the home and went there intending to steal it. They never found any drugs.
Ramey was also convicted in the killings and sentenced to death. His execution is scheduled for next week.
Norman was arrested about five months after the murders while trying to cross back into the United States from Mexico.

He later pleaded guilty to capital murder, leaving a jury to decide whether he would be sentenced to death. The U.S. Supreme Court denied a request from Norman’s attorneys Wednesday to stop the execution.
In his final moments, Norman lay on a thin mattress atop a steel table and looked toward a window. His sister, two of his children and a friend were there watching him.
A table fitted with restraints holds down death row prisoners while they are given a lethal injection at Huntsville Unit (Walls Unit) in Huntsville, Texas. (Greg Smith/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images)
After receiving a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, Norman took a couple of deep breaths, appeared to yawn and made several snoring sounds. He then stopped moving.
A physician examined him about 30 minutes later, and Norman was pronounced dead at 6:44 p.m.
KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL
No relatives or friends of the three people he killed witnessed the execution.
Norman was the fifth inmate executed in Texas this year.
Stacey Humphreys. (Georgia Department of Corrections)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Another execution scheduled for Wednesday was halted in Georgia, where Stacey Humphreys, a man convicted of killing two real estate agents, had been set to die. A judge stopped the execution in a late-night decision Tuesday after Humphreys' lawyers requested a delay over a new state law that gives victims of childhood abuse the opportunity to have their sentences reduced.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Pope Leo XIV receives 'symbolic’ sphere in charity's push for AI to 'protect human dignity'
summary: Photos show Pope Leo XIV receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" glass sculpture as 70 leaders prepare to draft the Codex Humanitatis on AI ethics.
story: Olivier Francois, president and chairman of Saint Peter for Humanity, speaks to Fox News Digital about giving Pope Leo XIV a "symbolic" artwork in its push to "protect human dignity" and establish "what should stay human in the age of AI."
A charity presented Pope Leo XIV with a unique piece of artwork in its push to "protect human dignity" and establish "what should stay human in the age of AI," an official told Fox News Digital.

Photos released by Saint Peter for Humanity captured the pope receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" — a green, Murano glass sculpture that "incorporates handwritten passages from his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, reflecting on human dignity, vulnerability, solidarity, conscience and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence" — during his General Audience in early September.

The presentation came as Saint Peter for Humanity said it is gearing up next week to gather 70 leaders in New York City to "begin drafting the Codex Humanitatis, an independent initiative inspired by Pope Leo XIV’s call to safeguard human dignity as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly powerful and influential in people’s lives."

"We recognize the benefits of AI. We just believe again that there is another force that should belong to that conversation; that other force is humanity," Olivier Francois, the organization’s president and chairman, told Fox News Digital. "So the Codex Humanitatis, which is our initiative, starts from that simple idea. AI should serve people, protect human dignity, expand human potential and advance common good."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL
The "Sphere of Humanity" glass sculpture is presented to Pope Leo XIV on Sept. 2, 2026, at the Vatican. (Vatican Media)

"So what are we going to do in New York? We are going to gather 70 Nobel laureates, artists, thinkers, philanthropists, technology and AI experts, obviously that's important, and we will ask them maybe the hardest question of our times, you know, as artificial intelligence grows even more powerful, what must remain human?" Francois added. "So obviously, before we head over to machines, we should be clear about what we value most in ourselves. So we will try to define what being human means and what should stay human in the age of AI. So this is a little bit of the initiative we shared with Pope Leo while presenting the sphere and this symbolic gift."

The sphere, based on an original design by Italian architect and designer Gae Aulenti, contains four handwritten passages from Pope Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas, including, "In the era of artificial intelligence, when human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human."

The pope wrote in the encyclical released in May, "Each generation inherits the task of shaping its own era, of guiding history to become a place where the dignity of every person is safeguarded, justice is promoted and fraternity is made possible," yet "every era also runs the risk of creating an inhumane and more unjust world.
OPINION: POPE LEO XIV’S AI WARNING SPEAKS DIRECTLY TO HOLLYWOOD’S MORAL CRISIS

Olivier Francois, the president and chairman of Saint Peter for Humanity, is seen standing to the left of Pope Leo XIV on Sept. 2, 2026, at the Vatican. Saint Peter for Humanity describes itself as a "nonprofit organization founded on the belief that every person is a member of one human family." (Vatican Media)

"For AI to respect human dignity and truly serve the common good, responsibility must be clearly defined at every stage: from those who design and develop these systems to those who use them and rely on them for concrete decisions," the pope wrote. "In many cases, however, the internal processes leading to a result remain opaque, making it harder to assign responsibility and correct errors. This is where accountability becomes crucial: the possibility of identifying who must ‘account’ for decisions, justify them, monitor them, and, when necessary, challenge them and remedy any harm caused.

"Calling for prudence, rigorous evaluation and even, at times, a slower pace in adopting AI does not mean opposing progress; instead, it is an exercise of responsible care for the human family. This need is all the more urgent given the frequent imbalance between the speed of technological growth and the slower development of awareness, norms, safeguards and institutions capable of governing its effects," the pope also said. "It is not enough to invoke ethics in the abstract; robust legal frameworks, independent oversight, informed users and a political system that does not abdicate its responsibility are required. Otherwise, change will be governed only by technocratic thinking and presented as necessary and inevitable, ultimately imposing rules shaped by those who control data, infrastructure and computing power."

Saint Peter for Humanity said in a statement about its New York gathering, "Working across ten groups, participants will develop a first draft of the Codex focused on issues including the future of work, accountability, information integrity, human oversight and the protection of children and families."

Pope Leo XIV arrives to lead his traditional Wednesday General Audience at St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City on Oct. 15, 2025. In May, the pope released his first encyclical, the Magnifica Humanitas. (Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"The draft will then enter a global consultation process before being refined into a final set of principles. Saint Peter for Humanity plans to engage governments, companies and institutions in translating those principles into practice, including through engagement at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos," the nonprofit added.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Memphis mom says Trump brought peace to streets as Democratic DA battles task force oversight
summary: A petition nearing 10,000 signatures demands DA Steve Mulroy drop his fight against Donald Trump's Memphis Safe Task Force accountability measures.
story: Memphis mother Dalisia Ballinger credits President Trump’s crime crackdown with silencing gunfire in her neighborhood and sounds off on the growing transparency battle surrounding task force cases.
A Memphis mother says President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown silenced the gunfire that years of pleas to local leaders could not and finally allowed her children to play outside.

"For once, I’m walking to my mailbox and it’s quiet," Dalisia Ballinger told Fox News Digital. "I’m hearing the birds chirp. I’m hearing the birds sing. I’m seeing children play in the middle of the street. I’m seeing fathers playing football."

The striking turnaround turned Ballinger, a former journalist and violent-crime victim, into one of the most outspoken supporters of the Memphis Safe Task Force as the operation marks one year on the ground.

It also put her at the center of a growing clash with Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy, a Democrat whose lawsuit against two new state oversight laws has sparked a petition demanding that he abandon the legal fight and disclose how his office handles cases generated by the task force.
FORMER CHICAGO DETECTIVE SAYS ONE CITY'S MURDER PLUNGE OFFERS WINDY CITY CRIME BLUEPRINT
A Memphis Police Department officer, right, patrols with members of the National Guard, Friday, Oct. 10, 2025, in Memphis, Tenn. (George Walker IV/AP Photo)
"Public safety should not be up for debate," Ballinger said. "I don’t care if you are a Republican. I don’t care if you are a Democrat."

Trump established the multi-agency operation through a presidential memorandum on Sept. 15, 2025, ordering federal, state and local authorities to coordinate against street and violent crime in Memphis. The task force is led by the U.S. Marshals Service and includes mobilized members of the Tennessee National Guard.
The White House said Tuesday that the operation had produced 12,747 arrests as of Sept. 15, including 131 homicide arrests, 1,276 firearms arrests and 1,408 arrests of known gang members.
The administration also credited the task force with taking 2,160 illegal guns off the streets and recovering 189 missing children.
FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN

President Donald Trump speaks during an event to sign a memorandum to send federal resources to Memphis, Tennessee, for a surge against local crime, in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 15, 2025. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Overall crime in Memphis fell nearly 36% compared with the previous year, while murders dropped 36%, robberies fell 42% and vehicle thefts plunged 57%, according to figures released by the White House. City data had already shown crime falling before the task force arrived, and the statistics do not establish how much of the decline resulted directly from the federal surge.
"That era is over. President Trump rejected the excuses, restored law and order, and once again proved that decline is a choice," the White House said.
FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%
Ballinger said the change became personal when her children could play outdoors without the constant fear that had gripped her neighborhood.

She recalled a shooting four houses away in which she said roughly 30 gunshots struck a home occupied by a grandmother and her grandchildren. The family never returned, she said, leaving the property overtaken by grass and weeds.
TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN 'WORKING' AS CITY SEES HOMICIDES PLUMMET 43% SINCE 2025: SLAIN INTERN'S MOM

"We’ve been begging for years for our local leaders for assistance and for help," Ballinger said. "My children deserve peace, and with the Memphis Safe Task Force being here, we’ve finally been able to get that peace."
Now, she and other supporters argue the operation’s arrests mean little if prosecutors later reduce or dismiss cases without explaining why.
PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT'
Federal law enforcement officers stand at the intersection of Beale St. and N. Second St., Wednesday, Oct. 8, 2025, in Memphis. (George Walker IV/AP Photo)
A Change.org petition titled "Stop Memphis DA From Protecting Criminals" had gathered nearly 10,000 verified signatures Wednesday.

The petition calls on Mulroy to drop a May lawsuit challenging the Memphis Safe Task Force Accountability Act and a separate law that authorizes the Tennessee attorney general to audit his office’s decisions in task force cases.

The accountability law requires Mulroy’s office to submit a report every 10 business days when it settles or dismisses a charge arising from the task force. The second law allows the state attorney general to review prosecutorial decisions in those cases and ask the Tennessee Supreme Court to appoint a temporary prosecutor.
PRIMARY SHOWDOWN: CONSERVATIVE FIREBRAND MARSHA BLACKBURN EYES GOVERNOR'S OFFICE IN TENNESSEE
Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy is challenging two Tennessee laws that increase oversight of his office’s handling of Memphis Safe Task Force cases. (Fox News Digital)

Mulroy argues that both laws unconstitutionally single out Shelby County, intrude on the discretion of a locally elected prosecutor and burden his staff with duplicative reporting. His office said it already reports case outcomes under existing Tennessee law.

"These bills target Shelby County unfairly and infringe on the rights of Shelby County voters," Mulroy said when the lawsuit was filed. He has characterized the dispute as a battle over whether Shelby County voters or state officials in Nashville control the district attorney’s office.
Petition supporters see the lawsuit differently.

"Thanks to President Trump, the Memphis Safe Task Force has delivered more for this city in one year than anyone thought possible," Ballinger, one of the petition's leading voices, said in a statement. "While federal, state, and local agents risk their lives taking criminals off our streets, DA Mulroy is fighting in court to hide how his office is undermining this task force."
President Donald Trump arrives to participate in a roundtable discussion on public safety at a Tennessee Air National Guard Base, Monday, March 23, 2026, in Memphis. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo)

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., and Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor previously pressed Mulroy for details after his office reported that 430 of 514 felony cases resolved in December 2025 ended without prison time and that 166 of the cases were categorized as violent. The lawmakers said the figures left unanswered how many defendants in violent cases received no prison sentence. Mulroy has accused his Republican critics of distorting crime data for political purposes.
Ballinger rejected the claim that the petition is merely a partisan campaign against a Democratic prosecutor.
"We have children. We have regular people that might not even be into politics," she said. "We deserve peace. Whether it’s on the East Coast, the West Coast or South, we all deserve peace."
MISSISSIPPI DISTRICT ATTORNEY JODY OWENS RESIGNS AFTER PLEADING GUILTY IN FEDERAL BRIBERY CASE: REPORT
Some Memphis residents think the police department, Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers and FBI are effectively fighting crime. (Fox News)

The task force has also drawn fierce opposition. The ACLU of Tennessee and several Memphis residents have accused agents of aggressive policing and retaliation against people who record law enforcement.
Four residents filed a federal lawsuit this year alleging harassment, unlawful arrests and physical mistreatment while exercising their First Amendment rights.
The allegations have not been proven in court, while task force supporters point to thousands of arrests and sharply falling crime numbers as evidence the operation is working.
Ballinger said legitimate complaints should be reviewed, but she does not believe they justify dismantling an operation she credits with making her neighborhood livable again.
"I’m all for fairness, and I’m all for law and order," she said. "If we need to go back to the table [and] restructure so that people can feel safe, we can definitely put that on the board."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For Ballinger, the anniversary is measured less by government statistics than by what she can see and hear beyond her front door.
"It was noticeably enough to where it’s like, ‘Wow, there’s kids actually outside playing,’" she said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Mulroy’s office for comment.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: West Virginia woman charged in death of ill husband she left on toilet for 19 hours
summary: A West Virginia woman allegedly left her husband who had dementia and Alzheimer's on a toilet for 19 hours without food or medication, leading to his death.
story: ‘Outnumbered’ panelists debate Virginia mom Karyann Parkinson’s controversial child neglect conviction. Parkinson was placed on the state’s child abuse registry for seven years after letting her 5-year-old son walk alone to a local pond.
A West Virginia woman is accused of leaving her frail and ailing husband on the toilet for 19 hours, an act investigators say contributed to his death.
Margaret Rog, 75, was arrested on Tuesday in connection with the death of her 76-year-old husband. She was charged with abuse or neglect of an incapacitated adult.

Authorities allege Rog had left her husband, who suffers from dementia, Alzheimer’s and legal blindness, on the toilet overnight last month, leading to serious health conditions that contributed to his death, the Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office said, according to WDTV.
Her husband went to the bathroom at around 3 p.m. on Aug. 20, but when he was finished doing his business, Rog was unable to help him off the toilet.
IOWA WOMAN DIED FOLLOWING HERNIA REPAIR AFTER NURSES DISMISSED PAINFUL POST-SURGERY SYMPTOMS: LAWSUIT
Margaret Rog was charged with abuse or neglect of an incapacitated adult. (West Virginia Department of Corrections)

According to investigators, instead of calling for help, the woman left her husband unattended and unresponsive for 19 hours without food, water or his prescribed medications, the sheriff's office said.
Deputies allege Rog watched her husband groan in pain but did not call anyone for help and later went to bed as her ailing husband remained stuck on the toilet, according to deputies.

At around 10 a.m. the following day, a speech therapist arrived for an in-home visit with Rog’s husband and found the man unresponsive and in dangerously poor condition, according to WDTV, citing court records.
The speech therapist then called an ambulance and the man was rushed to the hospital.
Margaret Rog had left her husband, who suffers from dementia, Alzheimer’s and legal blindness, on the toilet overnight. (Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office)
He was then diagnosed with several conditions, including heart failure, respiratory failure, pulmonary embolism, hypernatremia, sepsis and rhabdomyolysis.
The man was also found to have wounds on his backside, shortness of breath and an altered mental status, according to court records.
He died in the hospital on Aug. 31.
Investigators said the elderly man’s condition and injuries linked to being left on the toilet were "significant contributing factors" to his death, WDTV reported.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH
The ill man died in the hospital on Aug. 31. (Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office)

Rog allegedly made statements investigators described as self-incriminating to law enforcement, adult protection services and family members over the course of the investigation, according to court documents.
The woman allegedly suggested she was aware of her husband’s need for assistance but deliberately opted against offering any help.
She pleaded not guilty in court on Tuesday and posted a $75,000 bond.

title: WATCH: Handcuffed inmate breaks free, punches deputy in wild courthouse escape attempt
summary: Video shows Timothy Reaggle allegedly slipping out of his handcuffs and punching a bailiff in an attempt to escape after his sentencing hearing at the Columbiana County Courthouse.
story: Video released by the Columbiana County Sheriff’s Office shows Timothy Reaggle allegedly slipping out of his handcuffs, punching a bailiff and racing toward the courthouse exit before deputies stopped him.
Wild courthouse video appears to show a newly sentenced Ohio man slipping out of his handcuffs, punching a bailiff and making a desperate run for the exit before deputies stopped his escape.

Timothy J. Reaggle, 20, of Wellsville, allegedly attacked two Columbiana County Sheriff's Office deputies Monday shortly after learning he would spend a year in prison in a separate case, according to local reports.
Columbiana County Sheriff Brian McLaughlin told WFMJ that both deputies suffered broken bones but have since been released from the hospital.

Video released by the sheriff's office shows a deputy escorting Reaggle down a hallway after his sentencing. Reaggle then suddenly breaks free of his handcuffs and allegedly punches the deputy before sprinting away.
ESCAPED INMATE'S BID FOR FREEDOM COMES TO CRASHING END AFTER COORDINATED MANHUNT CLOSES IN
Video shows Timothy J. Reaggle sliding down courthouse steps as he races toward the exit during an alleged escape attempt. (Columbiana County Sheriff's Office)
As he runs down the hallway, Reaggle is seen crashing into another deputy, knocking him to the ground.
Reaggle then allegedly headed toward the courthouse exit, where video shows him sliding down the steps and racing toward the front doors before he was subdued with a Taser and taken into custody.
The video also shows people rushing to assist the injured deputies. One deputy was later seen lying on the floor, bleeding from the head and holding a paper towel against his face, according to WFMJ.
Reaggle had just been sentenced to one year in prison in a case dating to Feb. 14, 2025, according to WKBN.
He pleaded guilty in July to charges including aggravated burglary, aggravated assault, aggravated menacing, failure to comply and two misdemeanor counts of assault.
LOUISIANA SHERIFF CHARGED AFTER TOILET JAILBREAK LET 10 INMATES ESCAPE IN LOCKUP FIASCO
Video shows Timothy J. Reaggle allegedly breaking free of his handcuffs while being escorted through an Ohio courthouse following his sentencing. (Columbiana County Sheriff's Office)
McLaughlin said Reaggle is being held at the Columbiana County Jail and will eventually be transported to state prison.
Reaggle is also awaiting potential new charges stemming from the courthouse incident.

Deputies stopped Timothy J. Reaggle before he could escape the Columbiana County courthouse after he allegedly attacked two deputies. (Columbiana County Sheriff's Office)
According to WFMJ, McLaughlin said those charges are expected to include assault on a police officer and felony escape.

title: Maryland family speaks out after ‘4-foot-long’ rabid beaver attacks 13-year-old boy
summary: Family said a beaver attacked without provocation at Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County before testing positive for rabies.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The family of a 13-year-old boy who was viciously attacked by a rabid beaver in Maryland has spoken out about the incident, describing the animal as a massive, four-foot-long adult.
The July 26 incident was the first of three rabid beaver attacks that prompted Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County to close, according to the family's GoFundMe.
The teen was identified as Dominick Cebula by WUSA 9.
Dominick was swimming and looking at fish underwater in a designated area when the beaver suddenly struck his chest and latched onto him, the family said in their online fundraiser.
RABID BAT FOUND NEAR ZOO RESTAURANT SPARKS URGENT PUBLIC HEALTH WARNING: 'EXTREMELY SERIOUS'
Dominick Cebula, left, and his brother at Cunningham Falls State Park about 10 minutes before Dominick was attacked by a rabid beaver. (Alishia Cebula )
The family said the unprovoked attack unfolded in front of the boy's mother and younger brother, who watched in horror from the shore.

"This 4-foot-long beaver (not a cute little cuddly beaver — this thing was as big as his 8-year-old brother) came out of nowhere from the deep of the lake, beelined straight toward D, and began biting and attacking him," Dominick's aunt, Leigh Cebula, said.
"He did not provoke it, poke it, or mess with it in any way. This was completely unprovoked."
A beaver swimming in a creek.  (Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP Photo, File)
Dad Jeff Cebula told WUSA 9 the beaver began shaking its head and refused to let go.

"He grabbed its head and a leg, and he tried to get it off of him," Jeff said. "At that point, he kind of felt that it was locked onto him. And then it started shaking its head, kind of like a dog would do."
Dominick eventually managed to pull the beaver off his chest and tried to back away with his hands raised, his dad said.
The boy’s family said he fought off the beaver twice before being airlifted to Johns Hopkins Hospital for treatment. (Alishia Cebula )
The beaver then lunged at him again and bit his right hand, prompting Dominick to fight it off a second time.
He was promptly airlifted to Johns Hopkins Hospital, where doctors began treating his wounds and administering rabies post-exposure treatment.
"It was so traumatic. He was lifeflighted to Johns Hopkins because the paramedics were worried his lung was punctured. Luckily it wasn't," Dominick's mother, Alishia Cebula, told Fox News Digital.
The boy is now recovering well after undergoing surgery earlier this month.
NORTH CAROLINA WARNS MOBILE PETTING ZOO VISITORS OF RABIES EXPOSURE AFTER BABY GOATS TEST POSITIVE
Dominick’s younger brother had just left the water to retrieve his goggles when the beaver attacked his older brother, according to the family. (Alishia Cebula )

"He is doing much better. He just had surgery on 9/4 to repair a severed nerve in his finger," Alishia said. "He had a lot of appointments, especially with the rabies vaccines he had to get. Thank God for the vaccine.
"Luckily, we're getting to the end of this traumatic event."
Leigh added that the incident happened in an area where the family had swum for years and had never spotted beavers before.
After the attack, the beaver was euthanized after testing positive for rabies. Swimming access to Hunting Creek Lake at the park was closed soon afterward.
Dominick Cebula underwent surgery to repair a severed nerve in his finger and received rabies post-exposure treatment after the attack. (Alishia Cebula )
The incident marked the first in a series of three attacks at the park.
On Aug. 5, a 19-year-old fisherman was bitten in the ankle by a beaver.
