title: Putin, Xi and Iran's Pezeshkian descend on India for high-stakes BRICS summit amid escalating global tensions
summary: Presidents of Iran, Russia and China converge on New Delhi for the BRICS summit as India navigates competing interests amid Middle East and Ukraine wars.
story: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discusses the August jobs report, construction and manufacturing, Operation Economic Outcast, China and more on 'My View with Lara Trump.'

All eyes will be on New Delhi this weekend, as the presidents of Iran, Russia and China gather in India for the 18th BRICS summit. The meeting comes at a critical time as conflicts roil the Middle East and Europe, putting the bloc to one of its biggest tests since its founding 20 years ago.

The Sept. 12-13 summit comes more than six months after the Middle East war broke out between the U.S. and Iran, and at a time when regional tensions are again spiking. It follows the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit earlier this month, where several of the same leaders met.

The BRICS alliance was established in 2006 by founding members Brazil, Russia, India and China, and has since expanded to include nations such as Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
INDIA'S MODI-IRAN MEETING COMES AMID US WARNINGS OF SANCTIONS ON TEHRAN'S TRADING PARTNERS

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (L) holds a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian (R) on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31, 2026. (Press Information Bureau (PIB)/Anadolu via Getty Images)

At the forefront are Iran-India relations, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Prime Minister Narendra Modi likely to highlight trade, connectivity, energy cooperation and regional developments. The two leaders are meeting less than two weeks after reaffirming their "longstanding" strategic partnership.

In the face of an economic onslaught from Washington, Tehran has been working to deepen ties with Moscow and Beijing. In its latest attempt at securing a critical economic lifeline, Iran is seeking membership in the BRICS New Development Bank. The effort comes as many of Iran's largest remaining economic partners, including China, India, Russia and the UAE, will all be represented in New Delhi, giving Tehran a rare opportunity to engage several key trading partners collectively, just as the U.S. ramps up sanctions pressure.
CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS

Also in focus is China. President Xi Jinping will be visiting India for the first time in seven years. The high-stakes trip marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between India and China after a deadly military clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border. A bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi is expected to focus on maintaining that normalization while expanding economic engagement, making it one of the summit's most closely watched sidelines meetings.
Then there is Russia. President Vladimir Putin met Modi on Friday in a pre-summit bilateral meeting. It marks Putin's first trip to India since the Ukraine war began four years ago.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin (L) shakes hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi (R) during their meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on Sept. 11, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Energy and defense are expected to dominate the agenda after the Russian president criticized American tariffs as "illegal" and "unacceptable."

Just earlier this week, the Kremlin touted expanding energy ties, saying India's imports of Russian energy have reached a "new record" every month. Moscow has also said Russia understands India's position on the war in Ukraine and that it "to a great extent corresponds" with Russia's own position, while calling on India to facilitate a peaceful resolution.
IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS
Traffic moves along a street past a hoarding, displayed ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 9, 2026. (Photo by Sajjad Hussain/AFP via Getty Images)

The meeting also comes days after Putin publicly welcomed the UAE’s role in facilitating discussions over the Ukraine war, highlighting Abu Dhabi's increasingly influential diplomatic role as another major BRICS participant.
Saudi Arabia will also be watched after Iran-backed Houthi militia renewed attacks on its cities earlier this week.

Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia have become increasingly central to India's Gulf strategy. The summit also comes as New Delhi attempts to navigate widening divisions between Tehran and Abu Dhabi after the UAE cut off commercial and financial dealings with Iran. The suspension has already squeezed Indian exporters, as Dubai has long served as a key commercial hub for India's trade with Iran, giving India a direct economic incentive.

The BRICS summit will be a major test of India's diplomatic mettle in more ways than one, as the nation finds itself balancing competing interests from Washington, Tehran, Moscow, Beijing and the Gulf while trying to forge unity among BRICS members.

"New Delhi’s leadership of BRICS is ultimately an exercise in managing contradiction. The biggest challenge is to ensure BRICS remains a platform for advancing Global South priorities rather than becoming an arena for great-power rivalry, Harsh V. Pant, vice president at Observer Research Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "New Delhi is trying to keep the focus on practical cooperation — from energy security to connectivity and development — rather than ideological confrontation."
FROM BEAR HUGS TO HANDSHAKES: HOW INDIA LOST ITS EDGE WITH TRUMP WHILE PAKISTAN QUIETLY GAINED GROUND
Xi, Putin and Modi at BRICS. (MAXIM SHIPENKOV/Pool via REUTERS)

Building a unified position among BRICS members will be a complex task for India, especially given the sharp geopolitical divergences among member states, such as the U.S-China rivalry, the Russia-Ukraine war and tensions involving Iran, Israel and the UAE. Modi will have to balance championing his own priorities with the summit's, as well as toeing the line to avoid an anti-U.S. tilt.
"The balancing act reflects India's broader foreign policy, which seeks to maintain strong ties with Washington while continuing to engage Moscow, Beijing and Tehran," Pant said.
Throughout the conflict, India has sought to position itself as a voice for dialogue while avoiding taking sides, emphasizing themes of resilience, sustainability, cooperation and innovation.
But experts warn that failure to reach consensus would expose the limits of the expanded BRICS grouping, whose broader membership has also imported longstanding regional rivalries.

President Donald Trump (R) shakes hands with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting at the G7 Summit on June 17, 2026, in Evian-les-Bains, France. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Though major Western powers are absent, analysts say the alliance is not to be dismissed. Every ceasefire in this conflict has involved mediation by BRICS members or partners, and leaders gathering in New Delhi are expected to explore whether the forum can once again provide diplomatic momentum after recent attempts to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran stalled.

"Hosting the BRICS summit in New Delhi offers India an important opportunity to demonstrate the logic of its multi-alignment at a time when global politics is becoming increasingly polarized, "Pant said. "By bringing together countries such as China, Russia, Iran and the Gulf states while simultaneously deepening its partnerships with the United States and the Quad, India is signaling that it does not accept the binary choices imposed by great-power rivalry."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The stakes extend beyond diplomacy as disruptions from the war have disproportionately affected developing nations. India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, has already suffered energy and inflation hits.

"The real measure of India’s success will therefore be its ability to keep BRICS sufficiently inclusive and functional to address Global South priorities while preventing geopolitical divisions from paralyzing the grouping," Pant said.
Kyra Colah works as a Writer and Associate Producer for Fox News.

title: Rubio takes behind-the-scenes role on Iran war, while keeping his options open for the future
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on.
story: WASHINGTON — The talks to end the Iran war had hit a snag.

Vice President JD Vance had flown to Pakistan for negotiations with the Iranians, a sign that the two sides had narrowed their differences and the White House might be poised to announce a breakthrough.

As the marathon April meeting unfolded, though, U.S. negotiators began to worry: It looked like the Iranians were changing the terms of a potential deal. So, during a pause, they phoned Secretary of State Marco Rubio to get a “steer” on what they should do next, an administration official with direct knowledge of the matter said in an interview.
Rubio agreed that they couldn’t accept Iran’s offer, the official said. There would be no deal.

Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on. Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff are the main protagonists in the push to end both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

The arrangement is an unusual one. Past secretaries of state commanded the spotlight when it came to war and peace. Henry Kissinger won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1973 for negotiating a ceasefire in the Vietnam War during the Nixon administration. John Kerry, in the Obama administration, flew back and forth between Washington and the Middle East as he tried in vain to broker a peace deal between the Israelis and Palestinians.
Still, Rubio has been a hidden hand throughout, helping craft the Trump administration’s strategy while privately advising the officials who play a more public role in the peace talks.

He holds a unique place in the Cabinet, one of the most expansive in the modern presidency. Rubio doubles as national security adviser — first in an acting capacity, now permanent — meaning he has a spacious office in the West Wing and gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members.

This account is based on interviews with 12 present and former administration officials and others close to Rubio and the White House. Many spoke on condition of anonymity to talk freely about internal policy and political dynamics.

“The reason that the American people perhaps don’t see Secretary Rubio as front and center on Iran is because he really does have the rest of the world to worry about and pays enormous attention to the Western Hemisphere and our European allies,” White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told NBC News. “President Trump is so busy and active around the world, it takes more than one person. So, Secretary Rubio is leading the other efforts around the world that are so important to America’s stability and future promise.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

Trump has given Rubio wide latitude, allowing America’s top diplomat to be selective when it comes to the public parts of the job. Rubio was more visible in the early phase of the Iran war than in the later stages. That could prove advantageous down the road.

Polls show widespread American disenchantment with the conflict. As public opinion hardens, Rubio may be better positioned to sidestep any political backlash than Vance, who has attended futile rounds of peace talks in far-flung locales.

Rubio has said publicly that he currently has no plans to run in 2028, and two people familiar with the matter have told NBC News he has also said that privately. He has acknowledged behind closed doors that the landscape may be tough for Republicans in 2028 and suggested that a presidential run in 2032 or 2036 may be more promising, a person close to him said.
But Rubio’s comments don’t close the door completely. A second person close to him said that he has not ruled out a potential 2028 presidential run, but he is not discussing his future plans.
“Nobody knows what he’s going to do,” the source said. “Political calculation does not factor into literally anything that he’s doing right now.”

Another consideration is personal. Rubio has also said privately that after nearly three decades in public office he may want to take a job in the private sector when Trump’s term ends, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.

His financial disclosure form shows his net worth to be no more than $240,000 apart from his house, listed in a range between $1 million and $5 million. Those are modest sums in an administration packed with officials worth $100 million or more.
Rubio could readily land a lucrative job that would be a boon to himself, his wife and their four children if he sat out the race, and at 55, he is young enough to mount a campaign later on.
Relationship with Trump

Once angry rivals, Rubio and Trump have developed a good rapport. Rubio may be in and out of the Oval Office five or six times a day, a White House official told NBC News. Both love sports, and they’ve been overheard jawing about baseball batting averages or a knockout punch in the latest mixed martial arts match, the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a prepared statement: “As President Trump says, Marco Rubio will go down as one of the greatest Secretaries of State in history. The president and Secretary Rubio have successfully restored American dominance on the world stage and are relentlessly working to advance our foreign policy interests.”

After spending 14 years in the Senate, Rubio grasps the politics and legislative tactics needed to pass bills into law and will advise the president on ways to push his agenda through Congress, the official said.

“I can think of many times in which we’re talking about whatever he [Trump] is focused on that day and he’ll say, ‘What do you think, Marco?’ I’ve heard that more times than I can count,” a person close to the White House said. “They jell well together. I’ve seen people who don’t jell well with the president, and Marco is not one of those people.”

Rubio’s influence in the peace talks is largely behind the scenes. Witkoff checks in with him before agreeing to attend negotiating sessions, takes guidance before meetings and briefs him afterward, the administration official said.

Last weekend, the two men spoke by phone multiple times about an escalating conflict involving Iran and Yemen. On Saturday, Witkoff reached Rubio while the secretary of state was at the University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville, watching his son play for the Gators, the official said.

Leaving the Senate last year to work for Trump was a gamble for Rubio. The two faced off in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, where they one-upped each other in schoolyard taunts. Trump derided the Florida lawmaker as “Little Marco.” Rubio mocked the New York businessman’s hand size.
Time and pragmatic politics have transformed the rivalry into a partnership. The Senate confirmed Rubio by a vote of 99-0, a feat that has impressed even Trump.

Earlier this month, Rubio met with heads of state in Latin America as he sought to combat illegal immigration and drug trafficking.
The son of Cuban émigrés, he is also driving the administration’s effort to transform Cuba and bring an end to the regime in Havana.
If he can nudge Venezuela and Cuba toward democratic governance, that could be an enviable legacy for a secretary of state who is nursing presidential ambitions.

Another possibility would be for Rubio to become Vance’s running mate, something he would be inclined to do if asked, this person said. Trump himself has suggested the two men pair up in 2028, and his opinion counts given his grip on the Republican base.
Trump likes to ask people privately who they think should be the GOP nominee.

“If he’s serious about running, he would have to say so reasonably soon,” the White House official said. “Once you’re elected, you never really get rid of that bug. Ultimately, if there’s an opportunity and an opening, you’d be almost fighting your instincts not to do it.”

title: White House withdraws Trump’s nominee to lead ICE
summary: The White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday.
story: The White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday.
The White House did not say in the notice why Schroyer’s nomination was withdrawn.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately provide a response about the withdrawal, but a spokesperson said a statement from the agency is forthcoming.
Schroyer is a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and he was the secretary’s top pick to take over as director of ICE after Todd Lyons’ exit from the position in April.
Mullin was previously a U.S. senator for Oklahoma and knew Schroyer from that time.
Schroyer has decades of experience working in local law enforcement in the state, but not specifically with ICE.

Trump announced Schroyer’s nomination in a Truth Social post in June, saying, “Lance has firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets and, just like ME and our Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, he LOVES the men and women of ICE.”
Acting ICE Director David Venturella is expected to remain in his role leading the agency for the time being, according to an ICE spokesperson.

title: Most Americans think AI is doing more harm than good in schools
summary: Most American adults think artificial intelligence is going to do more harm than good in education, according to this month’s NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.
story: Most American adults think artificial intelligence is going to do more harm than good in education, according to this month’s NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.
And a growing share of U.S. adults believe schools that shun the technology will better help students grow than schools that embrace it.

The survey found that 53% of adults believe AI does more harm than good in K-12 education, compared with 27% who believe it does more good than harm. That’s similar to the 54% who said it does more harm than good in colleges and universities, while 24% said they believed it did more good than harm in higher education.

When it comes to preparing students for the future, 44% of respondents said a school that integrates AI tools into the classroom will better help students than a school that bans using it — down 9 percentage points from June 2025.
On the flip side, 56% of respondents said they believe a school that prohibits using AI will better help prepare students for the future, up 9 points since the June 2025 survey.
Respondents were mixed on what — if any — ways of using AI were acceptable for a student completing a school assignment.

Proofreading and editing was seen as the most acceptable use case among those tested, with 49% of adults saying that was OK. That was followed by 41% who said it is acceptable for students to use AI to help with researching and brainstorming and 38% who believed it is OK to use AI to organize or outline ideas.
About a third of respondents, 31%, said no AI use was acceptable for schoolwork. Just 7% said it was OK for students to have AI do writing and generate content for them.

The subject of AI use in the classroom is raging in school districts and on campuses across the country. Parents and advocates nationwide have raised concerns about AI use, saying it has stunted students’ educational growth, and some school districts have enacted restrictions.
New York City announced this month that the use of AI for students will be restricted until high school, with only limited use cases allowed then.
Melania Trump says young students 'need to learn' about AI

On Tuesday, first lady Melania Trump told NBC News that she believes it is important for students to get hands-on experience with AI, a technology that is likely to shape their futures far beyond the classroom.

“Of course, they need to be vigilant, as well,” she said. “But this is our future, and we need to guide them and teach them what is available. If not, they will stay behind, and we need to be the first, in [the] United States, to lead.”
The NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey surveyed 7,105 adults online from Aug. 20 to Sept. 1 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.

title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
summary: Researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science. The Tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian cloud forest.
story: For the first time in a century, researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science.

Leopardus tilcayo — or the tilcayo tiger cat — is slender and spotted, with rounded ears. It is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin. The species was described for the first time in the journal Current Biology on Thursday.

It’s rare to find a new, relatively large mammal. Unsurprisingly, most newly discovered animal species are small in size, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study and leads a wild cat conservation program called Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia (Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program).
“This time, it’s a cat. That’s really novel. And it hasn’t happened in 100 years,” she said. “No one else had named it. No one else had described it.”
The size of the Leopardus tilcayo population is not clear yet.

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” said Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work as a conservationist is funded by National Geographic. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”

title: Matthew Lillard ‘ashamed’ he returned to ‘Scream’ after Melissa Barrera fired for Israel-Gaza posts
summary: Matthew Lillard expressed regret on Tuesday over his decision to film “Scream 7” after actor Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise over her social media about the Israel-Gaza war, saying he was “on the wrong side of history.”
story: Matthew Lillard expressed regret on Tuesday over his decision to film “Scream 7” after actor Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise over her social media about the Israel-Gaza war, saying he was “on the wrong side of history.”

Video showed the actor speaking to fans during a Q&A at a 30th anniversary screening for the original “Scream” at a Regal movie theater in Austin, Texas. It’s unclear what the question was, as the video only shows Lillard speaking, but it appears to be related to celebrities taking stances on political topics.

Lillard described it as a “great question” and referred to the ongoing situation with singer Ed Sheeran, who is facing backlash after venues pressured him to drop Macklemore from his tour over his pro-Palestinian remarks.
“I don’t think it’s easy all the time,” he said, before referring to Barrera.

Barrera starred in “Scream 6” and was expected to return for the seventh installment of the hit horror franchise, but was fired in 2023. Spyglass Media Group, the production company behind the film, confirmed it had dropped Barrera after she shared Instagram posts condemning Israel.

According to a Variety report, Barrera’s post included references to Israel as a “colonized” land and reshared posts that accused Israel of “genocide and ethnic cleansing.” Another post said that “Western media only shows the (Israeli) side.”
“Why do they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself,” the post reportedly said.

Spyglass Media Group told Variety in a statement that it has zero tolerance for “antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form.” Barrera initially declined to comment, but later told the Associated Press that she was “grateful” for everything that had happened and felt it was an “awakening.”

“Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian— what started happening in Israel,” Lillard said. “It’s really f---ing bulls--- and really hard and she’s on the right side of history.”
“But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal,” he said.
The “Scream” actor’s remarks come days after rapper Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s tour over a speech and performance centered on his pro-Palestinian views.

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, said Monday that venues threatened to cancel Sheeran’s shows in response to the rapper saying “Free Palestine” on stage. Among those involved was New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who Macklemore accused of organizing a boycott against the rapper.
While talking about the consequences Barrerra suffered, Lillard said, “And when they start coming after your job, sometimes things are worth it.”

He noted that he “got called out” for returning to the “Scream” franchise in the same film Barrera was set to star in. Lillard described himself as being on “the wrong side of history” for that choice.

“I feel bad about that, I feel ashamed about that,” Lillard said. “Because in that moment I was so excited to go back that I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey and didn’t say no. And I’m embarrassed, and that’s the truth.”
“I still like being in the movie, but it may not have been the best idea,” he said.

title: Australian athlete apologizes after winning race despite involuntary bowel movement
summary: An Australian athlete apologized Thursday for continuing — and winning — her race in China over the weekend after experiencing an involuntary bowel movement during competition.
story: An Australian athlete apologized Thursday for continuing — and winning — her race in China over the weekend after experiencing an involuntary bowel movement during competition.
Joanna Wietrzyk, a 24-year-old from Melbourne, said she should have pulled off the track during the women’s 16-to-24 Hyrox event in Beijing on Saturday.
The athlete said she hadn’t felt any symptoms before the race that might have warned her about what was to come.
“I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” Wietrzyk said in statement.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”

Hyrox is a relatively new indoor sport that combines running and performing high-intensity exercises at various workout stations. It’s not an Olympic sport, but its backers hope it could make the Games in 2032 or 2036.

“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected,” Wietrzyk said. “I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.”
Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologized for the incident on Sunday and said organizers should have intervened immediately.
Wietrzyk’s time of 1:01:23 would have put her atop her division, but she has asked to “retroactively withdraw” from competition.

“On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned,” Wietrzyk said. “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

title: Rubio takes behind-the-scenes role on Iran war, while keeping his options open for the future
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on.
story: WASHINGTON — The talks to end the Iran war had hit a snag.

Vice President JD Vance had flown to Pakistan for negotiations with the Iranians, a sign that the two sides had narrowed their differences and the White House might be poised to announce a breakthrough.

As the marathon April meeting unfolded, though, U.S. negotiators began to worry: It looked like the Iranians were changing the terms of a potential deal. So, during a pause, they phoned Secretary of State Marco Rubio to get a “steer” on what they should do next, an administration official with direct knowledge of the matter said in an interview.
Rubio agreed that they couldn’t accept Iran’s offer, the official said. There would be no deal.

Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on. Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff are the main protagonists in the push to end both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

The arrangement is an unusual one. Past secretaries of state commanded the spotlight when it came to war and peace. Henry Kissinger won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1973 for negotiating a ceasefire in the Vietnam War during the Nixon administration. John Kerry, in the Obama administration, flew back and forth between Washington and the Middle East as he tried in vain to broker a peace deal between the Israelis and Palestinians.
Still, Rubio has been a hidden hand throughout, helping craft the Trump administration’s strategy while privately advising the officials who play a more public role in the peace talks.

He holds a unique place in the Cabinet, one of the most expansive in the modern presidency. Rubio doubles as national security adviser — first in an acting capacity, now permanent — meaning he has a spacious office in the West Wing and gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members.

This account is based on interviews with 12 present and former administration officials and others close to Rubio and the White House. Many spoke on condition of anonymity to talk freely about internal policy and political dynamics.

“The reason that the American people perhaps don’t see Secretary Rubio as front and center on Iran is because he really does have the rest of the world to worry about and pays enormous attention to the Western Hemisphere and our European allies,” White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told NBC News. “President Trump is so busy and active around the world, it takes more than one person. So, Secretary Rubio is leading the other efforts around the world that are so important to America’s stability and future promise.”

Trump has given Rubio wide latitude, allowing America’s top diplomat to be selective when it comes to the public parts of the job. Rubio was more visible in the early phase of the Iran war than in the later stages. That could prove advantageous down the road.

Polls show widespread American disenchantment with the conflict. As public opinion hardens, Rubio may be better positioned to sidestep any political backlash than Vance, who has attended futile rounds of peace talks in far-flung locales.

Rubio has said publicly that he currently has no plans to run in 2028, and two people familiar with the matter have told NBC News he has also said that privately. He has acknowledged behind closed doors that the landscape may be tough for Republicans in 2028 and suggested that a presidential run in 2032 or 2036 may be more promising, a person close to him said.
But Rubio’s comments don’t close the door completely. A second person close to him said that he has not ruled out a potential 2028 presidential run, but he is not discussing his future plans.
“Nobody knows what he’s going to do,” the source said. “Political calculation does not factor into literally anything that he’s doing right now.”

Another consideration is personal. Rubio has also said privately that after nearly three decades in public office he may want to take a job in the private sector when Trump’s term ends, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.

His financial disclosure form shows his net worth to be no more than $240,000 apart from his house, listed in a range between $1 million and $5 million. Those are modest sums in an administration packed with officials worth $100 million or more.
Rubio could readily land a lucrative job that would be a boon to himself, his wife and their four children if he sat out the race, and at 55, he is young enough to mount a campaign later on.
Relationship with Trump

Once angry rivals, Rubio and Trump have developed a good rapport. Rubio may be in and out of the Oval Office five or six times a day, a White House official told NBC News. Both love sports, and they’ve been overheard jawing about baseball batting averages or a knockout punch in the latest mixed martial arts match, the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a prepared statement: “As President Trump says, Marco Rubio will go down as one of the greatest Secretaries of State in history. The president and Secretary Rubio have successfully restored American dominance on the world stage and are relentlessly working to advance our foreign policy interests.”

After spending 14 years in the Senate, Rubio grasps the politics and legislative tactics needed to pass bills into law and will advise the president on ways to push his agenda through Congress, the official said.

“I can think of many times in which we’re talking about whatever he [Trump] is focused on that day and he’ll say, ‘What do you think, Marco?’ I’ve heard that more times than I can count,” a person close to the White House said. “They jell well together. I’ve seen people who don’t jell well with the president, and Marco is not one of those people.”

Rubio’s influence in the peace talks is largely behind the scenes. Witkoff checks in with him before agreeing to attend negotiating sessions, takes guidance before meetings and briefs him afterward, the administration official said.

Last weekend, the two men spoke by phone multiple times about an escalating conflict involving Iran and Yemen. On Saturday, Witkoff reached Rubio while the secretary of state was at the University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville, watching his son play for the Gators, the official said.

Leaving the Senate last year to work for Trump was a gamble for Rubio. The two faced off in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, where they one-upped each other in schoolyard taunts. Trump derided the Florida lawmaker as “Little Marco.” Rubio mocked the New York businessman’s hand size.

If he can nudge Venezuela and Cuba toward democratic governance, that could be an enviable legacy for a secretary of state who is nursing presidential ambitions.

Rubio’s statement to a Colombian radio station earlier this month that he currently has “no plans” to mount another campaign was not a hard-and-fast denial. Even if it was, it might not matter. When Rubio first ran for president, he made clear he was done with the Senate. And he sounded adamant.

title: How Canada and the E.U. are teaming up to counter Trump
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg to lay out how middle powers might counteract Trump’s hostility.
story: Around 3,700 miles separate the Gothic towers of Canada’s Parliament in Ottawa from the glass-fronted modern European Parliament building in eastern France.
But judging by the thunderous applause shaking the E.U. chamber Thursday, President Donald Trump’s threats are helping to close that distance.

Canada and Europe have long been close U.S. allies, benefiting from American military power and trading heft. But Trump has upended those relationships, waging trade wars against Canada and the E.U., while threatening to absorb Canada as America’s 51st state and take control of Greenland, Denmark’s autonomous Arctic territory.
Without a reliable partner in the White House, the spurned allies are now forging their own path.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged the world’s “middle powers” to join forces in a speech before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday to create “an alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices.”
The strategy in short: strength in numbers.
“I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners,” he stressed.

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney continued. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience. So no one — no one — can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

The remarks appeared aimed in part at Trump, though Carney did not name the president in his speech. The response in the room was a near-unanimous standing ovation from lawmakers representing the bloc’s 27 member countries.
Some European leaders, meanwhile, appear ready to grant Canada more favorable access to its closely guarded single market.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen caused a stir Wednesday when she suggested making Canada the E.U.’s first “associate member.” She also outlined an “alliance for the future” that would increase cooperation on defense, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and other tech.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

At a news conference Thursday, Carney stressed that Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member” of the European Union, a long and drawn-out process of regulatory alignment that can sometimes take decades for applicant countries.
“What matters is the substance,” he said of the associate membership proposal.

Carney has deep links to Europe, having served as governor of the Bank of England before his political homecoming propelled him to Canada’s leadership. He tapped into those ties Wednesday, bonding with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at an Everton soccer match.

title: DNA links Arizona man who died by suicide to 1987 cemetery murder of Navy veteran
summary: The DNA of an Arizona man who died by suicide earlier this year has connected him to the unsolved slaying of a Navy veteran whose body was dumped in a cemetery four decades ago, prosecutors said.
story: The DNA of an Arizona man who died by suicide earlier this year has connected him to the unsolved slaying of a Navy veteran whose body was dumped in a cemetery four decades ago, prosecutors said.

Orison James “Jim” Chafin was 54 when he was killed on Aug. 7, 1987, and investigators now believe the homicide was committed by Gary Wayne Billups, according to a statement issued Tuesday by Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes.
Billups was 68 when he died by suicide on June 24, days after he submitted DNA to investigators, authorities said.
Chafin’s body was found at Resthaven Cemetery in Glendale with his throat cut, officials said.

In the early-morning hours of Aug. 8, 1987, witnesses in a car driving through the cemetery spotted a parked midsized sedan, which then “fled across the dirt and sidewalk,” according to the AG’s statement.
Chafin’s body was found near where that suspicious car had been parked.
Chafin had been drinking on the afternoon and evening of Aug. 7 at Critters Lounge, about 2 miles from where his body was found, prosecutors said.
Detectives collected beer bottles and cigarette butts from that bar, and “testing produced three male DNA profiles,” which were then “entered into the national CODIS database,” the AG said.
The case remained unsolved for decades before cold-case investigators from the AG’s office and Glendale police took a fresh look at Chafin’s murder last year, Mayes said.
New interviews with surviving witnesses led investigators to Billups, “who had lived in Glendale in 1987 but was never interviewed by police at the time,” according to Mayes.

A witness placed the victim and suspect at the since-shuttered Critters Lounge, telling investigators that she remembered how  “victim James also got into a fight with Gary over James verbally attacking a subject named Mark who was not there to defend himself,” the AG said.
Billups voluntarily spoke to police on June 19 and denied knowing Chafin and “denied living in Glendale in 1987, despite arrest records placing him in the city in 1986 and 1987,” the AG said.
He provided a DNA sample, walked free that day and died by suicide five days later — all before “DNA results confirming the match were returned” on Aug. 6, state prosecutors said.

“Two other individuals investigated in connection with the case have also since died and could not be contacted further,” the AG’s statement said. “The Attorney General’s Office and the Glendale Police Department both consider this case closed.”

title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
summary: Researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science. The Tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian cloud forest.
story: For the first time in a century, researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science.

Leopardus tilcayo — or the tilcayo tiger cat — is slender and spotted, with rounded ears. It is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin. The species was described for the first time in the journal Current Biology on Thursday.

It’s rare to find a new, relatively large mammal. Unsurprisingly, most newly discovered animal species are small in size, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study and leads a wild cat conservation program called Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia (Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program).
“This time, it’s a cat. That’s really novel. And it hasn’t happened in 100 years,” she said. “No one else had named it. No one else had described it.”
The size of the Leopardus tilcayo population is not clear yet.

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” said Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work as a conservationist is funded by National Geographic. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”

title: Democratic senators request Pentagon provide ‘bare minimum’ on cost of Iran war
summary: Nearly the entire Democratic caucus in the Senate is demanding that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with a full accounting of the cost of the war in Iran along with related budget requests, as frustration grows that the Pentagon is not being forthcoming about the war and its fiscal impact.
story: WASHINGTON — Nearly the entire Democratic caucus in the Senate is demanding that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with a full accounting of the cost of the Iran war along with related budget requests, as frustration grows that the Pentagon is not being forthcoming about the conflict and its fiscal impact.

Forty-six Democratic senators sent a letter to Hegseth early Thursday demanding a detailed breakdown of the cost of military operations against Iran.  The letter was spearheaded by Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan.

While the Pentagon has provided some estimates, it has not detailed  the total cost of the war, including how much it would cost to repair damage to U.S. military bases, replace destroyed air and naval assets, and refurbish ships and aircraft ground down by seven months of war.

The lawmakers sent the letter as they consider a Pentagon request for $67 billion in additional funding and amid deepening frustration, among Democrats and some Republicans, over the direction of the war, which appears to be in a stalemate, and the caliber of information the Pentagon is providing members of Congress.

“Despite your stated needs, you have repeatedly refused to share basic information that previous administrations, Republican and Democratic, provided to the American public and Congress during times of war,” the letter states, citing the lack of Pentagon briefings for Congress or the media.

Only Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, who has faced ongoing questions about leaving the Democratic Party, declined to sign the letter. Fetterman said in a statement to NBC News that his record has been consistent.

“I’ve always been at odds with my fellow Democrats over how we hold Iran accountable. I’ll continue to remain an unapologetic supporter of efforts to confront the Iranian regime and its proxies,” he said.
The Pentagon didn’t immediately comment.

title: Texas abortion ban caused pregnant woman’s death, lawsuit says
summary: The family of a Texas woman who died from a pregnancy-related complications is suing state Attorney General Ken Paxton and the hospital where she was treated, claiming the state’s ban on most abortions killed her.
story: The family of a Texas woman who died of pregnancy-related complications is suing state officials and the hospital where she was treated, claiming the state’s ban on most abortions killed her.

Walker’s family filed a lawsuit in San Antonio on Tuesday, claiming that a doctor repeatedly denied her an abortion despite her having a medical emergency that would have legally permitted terminating the pregnancy.

The lawsuit names Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who is running for election to the U.S. Senate, the Texas Medical Board, which regulates the state’s medical professionals, the University of Texas Health Science ‌Center at ⁠San Antonio and several doctors who treated Walker before she died.

“For months, Ms. Walker had been asking for termination of her pregnancy — even though this was a wanted pregnancy — because she did not think she would survive the pregnancy. Tragically, she was right,” the lawsuit states. “An abortion at any point during her pregnancy would have saved her life.”
A representative for Paxton did not immediately return NBC News’ request for comment. The Texas Medical Board and the hospital system declined to comment.

The hospital where Walker was treated, University Health, said in a statement Thursday that it could not comment on Walker’s case specifically, but that its “priority is to provide medically appropriate and timely care.”

“In general, our clinicians make patient care decisions based on each patient’s clinical condition, applicable medical standards and legal requirements,” Elizabeth Allen, a spokesperson for the hospital, said in an email. “We take concerns about patient care seriously and review them through appropriate internal clinical and quality processes.”

In September 2024, Walker checked herself into the emergency room at University Health with symptoms of pre-eclampsia, a potentially deadly pregnancy complication, according to the lawsuit. Pre-eclampsia is characterized by high blood pressure and organ failure. It is a leading cause of death among mothers and babies in the United States.

The treatment for a severe case of the complication is immediate delivery of the child. However, at 20 weeks pregnant, delivery of Walker’s baby before full term would have been legally considered abortion in Texas.
Texas effectively banned all abortions in the state in 2024. Under the law, women can not have an abortion as soon as fetal cardiac activity is detected, which can be as early as five weeks.

There are no exceptions for case of rape, incest or fetal anomaly. However, under the law, a physician may perform an abortion when the mother has a life-threatening condition caused by the pregnancy.

The lawsuit alleges that when Walker showed those conditions and asked for an abortion, the doctors sent her home. The family is represented by lawyers affiliated with Abortion in America, an advocacy group, and the Marynell Maloney Law Firm.

Her family accused doctors of telling Walker “your baby is fine,” and blamed officials for imposing “a merciless blanket prohibition on abortion that intimidates doctors into ​inaction and breeds extreme fear among Texas’ medical establishment.”
Walker died in December of that year. She left behind a husband and teenage son.
“Tierra, she would have changed the world. And she’s changing it now,” Latanya Walker, one of Tierra Walker’s aunts, said at a press conference Wednesday.

title: Salvadorans with TPS don’t know how long their protections will last
summary: José Palma of the National TPS Alliance says wrong paperwork or advice can jeopardize future immigration status, as he argues immigrants here for 25 years should have a “permanent solution.”
story: HOUSTON — José Palma’s face lights up when he remembers leaving El Salvador in 1998 at the age of 23 for the U.S., with the dream of working, learning English and building a family.

Twenty-eight years later, his life is divided between paperwork, community hearings, and a family full of love and varying immigration statuses: Palma, who lives in Houston, has U.S. citizen children — two of whom are still young — and a wife who’s a legal permanent resident, and he’s a beneficiary of Temporary Protected Status, which allows eligible immigrants from certain countries to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation.

As the national coordinator of the National TPS Alliance, Palma has been answering a lot of questions from Salvadorans with TPS: Their immigration protections were set to expire last week, but the Department of Homeland Security announced that Salvadorans will retain TPS protections — including work authorization — for now until an announcement is made at a later date.

But there’s uncertainty among Salvadoran TPS holders about what could come next and what happens now with work permits or driver’s licenses that have expired or are about to expire. Immigrants from countries that have lost their TPS designation, including Haiti and Nicaragua, have lost their work permits and ability to be in the U.S. legally, and they face deportation.
Palma has lived under TPS protection since 2001.
“Everything we’ve built is in danger of collapsing,” he said. “Twenty-five years is not a short time. It’s a lifetime.”

Palma said that amid the uncertainty, Salvadoran TPS holders and their families have been dealing with real consequences: People are being asked not to return to work by their employers, families fear the loss of their health insurance and parents are unsure if they will be able to continue driving vehicles in the United States.
Advising caution
Palma recommended one thing to Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries: “Don’t panic or make decisions based on rumors,” he said.

The Trump administration has said that until it announces a decision, Salvadorans with TPS still have protection, so Palma’s advice is “to rely only on official sources, credible community organizations and established media” for accurate information.
One of the biggest points of confusion, Palma acknowledged, is whether Salvadoran TPS holders can continue working.

“DHS has said that people retain protection, but USCIS guidance for employers indicated that certain automatic work permit extensions were valid until Sept. 9,” Palma said, referring to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. “People should keep their USCIS letters, check their myUSCIS account and seek accredited legal advice before assuming which document applies to their case or employment.”

For those who have already received warnings from employers, Palma had this advice: “Do not resign or sign any documents you do not understand. Bring any official notifications you receive from USCIS to your employer and ask human resources to check the agency for updates regarding Form I-9. No one should decide the future of your immigration case based on an unverified comment, social media post or phone call.”

Unfortunately, some Salvadoran TPS holders have already been affected. Palma said that people who applied between January and March 2025 to renew their work permits haven’t received them. Some employers have told them not to return to work, and others have told them they can only work until a certain date.
“Driver’s licenses depend on immigration status, health insurance can be cut off and loans can be denied — the consequences go far beyond losing immigration protection or a work permit,” he said.
If the Trump administration decides to end TPS protections for Salvadorans, people don’t have to leave the country within 60 days, Palma emphasized.

“That period is the minimum protection period before a decision can take effect,” he said. “After that, each person must evaluate their case: There may be a family petition, asylum, another legal process or an immigration defense. The recommendation is to seek legal evaluation now and not wait for an emergency.”
What to do in the meantime

Salvadoran TPS holders should be gathering copies of their work permit, TPS certificate, passport, driver’s license, USCIS receipts, birth and marriage certificates, children’s medical and school records, proof of employment, and tax returns, Palma said.

He also said it’s important to identify a licensed immigration attorney or accredited organization. He urged people not to lie on any forms or submit applications for which they don’t qualify or give money to people who promise to “fix” their immigration status.

Palma also warned against signing documents without understanding them, giving access to bank accounts or personal information to strangers, or trusting a notary as if they were an immigration lawyer.

TPS holders should also avoid any legal problems or issues such as driving under the influence of alcohol, using false documents or committing acts that could jeopardize any future immigration status.
When asked what TPS holders should do if they’re stopped or approached by authorities, Palma said the important thing to do is “stay calm.”

“Bringing a copy of your identification or immigration documents can be helpful. If it’s an immigration officer, don’t sign any papers without knowing what they contain or without speaking to a lawyer,” he said. “Every case is different, but a signature obtained under duress can have serious immigration consequences.”
Temporary status for decades becomes a ‘whole life’

The National TPS Alliance estimates that about 170,000 Salvadorans are directly protected by TPS. However, Palma explained that the actual number of people affected is much higher when one includes U.S. citizen children, spouses, employers, churches, businesses and entire communities.

If TPS for Salvadorans is ended, “the impact would be immediate in cleaning, hotels, restaurants, kitchens and construction; there are also Salvadorans with TPS working in transportation, healthcare and professional occupations,” he said.
Palma was asked what he tells people who say that TPS is temporary and beneficiaries should return to their countries.
He said it’s important to understand the history of the program.

“It’s been renewed every 18 months, under both Democratic and Republican administrations, for 25 years. After all this time, we haven’t been given an opportunity to apply for permanent status,” he said. “So, the question is legal, but also moral: If someone has lived in the United States for 25 years with immigration status, is that really temporary? For many, 25 years is a whole life.”

“The least we deserve is the opportunity to continue our lives, as we have done all these years, but with permanent immigration status,” Palma said. “I want Democrats and Republicans to take this issue seriously, reach an agreement and find a permanent solution.”
An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

title: Stocks and bonds rally after Fed hikes rates and oil prices fall
summary: U.S. stock indexes rose sharply Thursday after the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in a bid to rein in rising inflation.
story: U.S. stock indexes rose sharply Thursday after the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in a bid to rein in rising inflation.
The S&P 500 soared 1.2% while the Nasdaq Composite surged 1.7%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 365 points, or 0.7%. The Russell 2000 index, which tracks small and midsize companies, rose 1%.
Gains across stock indexes were thanks to big jumps in tech shares, including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, Intel and AMD.
The jump in stocks also came alongside a rally in bonds, sending their yields lower, as the price of oil declined for a second straight day.

U.S. crude oil briefly fell below $100 per barrel for the first time since Friday, and Brent crude fell to as low as $101 after hitting $109 just two days earlier. However, as the afternoon went on, the decline in U.S. crude oil faded and it traded about flat around $102.

There was also positive economic news in the latest jobless claims report, which showed that filings for unemployment claims declined to the lowest level since July. However, this data could be an outlier because last week was a short holiday week.

U.S. Treasury bond yields fell as stock markets rose. After touching 5.02% on Wednesday, the 10-year Treasury yield declined to as low as 4.94%. The 30-year yield declined to as low as 5.29% after hitting 5.36% a day earlier.
Bond yields around the world also eased further after the Bank of England declined to raise interest rates and canceled plans to sell a tranche of longer-dated bonds.

The move across assets appeared to be helped by a renewed confidence in the Fed and its new chairman, Kevin Warsh. After Warsh’s first few speeches and statements sent bond yields soaring to multidecade highs and confused investors, Warsh’s Wednesday press conference drew praise for its clarity.
“Warsh’s press conference was coherent, confident and consistently hawkish without coming across as crazily so,” wrote Evercore ISI’s vice chairman Krishna Guha.
In central banker speak, hawkish typically refers to an official who supports higher rates to keep inflation in check.

“The Warsh Fed defied the Trump administration and preserved its credibility by following through on earlier signals” that it would hike rates, wrote ABN-AMRO economist Rogier Quaedvlieg in a report Thursday morning.
Warsh “threaded the needle very well,” wrote Northlight Asset Management Chief Investment Officer Chris Zaccarelli.

Meanwhile, oil’s decline was largely attributed to a report overnight that President Donald Trump would likely discuss the Iran war with Gulf leaders next week at the United Nations General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York.

Saudi Arabia is also reportedly making progress restoring up to half of its East-West oil pipeline capacity after the key artery was shuttered following an attack on the critical energy asset. The pipeline could be back in service within days, Bloomberg News reported.
NBC News was not able to immediately confirm the reporting.
Still, oil prices remain sharply elevated since the start of the year. U.S. and Brent crude oil prices are both trading more than 70% higher.

Retail gasoline prices climbed again Thursday by 7 cents to a national average price of $4.43 per gallon. Diesel prices also continued their surge, with the AAA national average jumping 8 cents to $6.39 per gallon. The average price of diesel is now up 93 cents from a month ago.

Yet Thursday’s market optimism could be short-lived. Fed officials warned Wednesday that the central bank likely needs to hike rates again before the end of the year. They also forecast another potential hike early next year.
Additionally, the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise rates on Thursday evening. Higher rates can often ripple across the global bond market.

title: Singer Duncan Sheik in ‘critical but stable’ condition and receiving care
summary: Tony Award-winning singer and songwriter Duncan Sheik is in “critical but stable” condition and receiving medical care, according to a statement posted to his Instagram account Wednesday evening.
story: Tony Award-winning singer and songwriter Duncan Sheik is in “critical but stable” condition and receiving medical care, according to a statement posted to his Instagram account Wednesday evening.
“Duncan is currently receiving medical care and remains in critical but stable condition,” the statement said.
“Out of respect for Duncan and our family, we will not be sharing further medical details at this time,” it added.
“We kindly ask for privacy during this incredibly difficult time and will provide updates when appropriate,” the statement continued. “Thank you for the continued love and support.”
It remains unclear where Sheik is receiving medical care or what his prognosis is.
Sheik, 56, is perhaps best known for his 1996 hit “Barely Breathing,” which remains at the top of his Spotify page three decades later.
The song earned him a Grammy nomination for best male pop vocal performance. He has released nine studio albums over his career, with the most recent in 2022.
In 2002, Sheik began writing music for the theater. That year, he composed the music for the New York Shakespeare Festival production of “Twelfth Night.”
But his biggest break came just years later, in 2006, with the success of “Spring Awakening” on Broadway, for which he co-wrote the music with Steven Sater.

His work on the breakout Broadway show earned him two Tony Awards: best orchestrations and best original score, which he shared with Sater. “Spring Awakening” also won best musical at the Tonys that year and earned a Grammy Award for best musical show album.
According to a 2012 Broadway World article, Sheik said he had been working on the music for a “Spring Awakening” film adaptation. It is unclear whether that project is still in the works.
The show’s off-Broadway revival begins previews on Nov. 27 and officially opens on Dec. 17.

Sheik kept composing for the theater after “Spring Awakening,” writing music for “Alice By Heart” (2012), “American Psycho” (2013), “The Taming of the Shrew” (2016) and “The Secret Life of Bees” (2019).

If you ever lose electricity or have a power outage, such as during a hurricane, you can use a portable power station to juice up devices and even appliances, you can also use one in your home to funnel power to devices where you don’t have easy access to a charging point or even at a campsite hundreds of miles from home.

Portable power stations are a safe and easy-to-use alternative to generators, with the benefit of charging right from a traditional power socket, or via solar power. How I picked the best portable power stations

I chose portable power stations based on advice from our experts, Mike Kreis, a product, sales and customer service specialist at REI and Josh Noble, the director of merchandise management at Batteries Plus; as well as the following criteria:

Watt-hours and wattage: “There are two specific numbers you should look for when considering a portable power station,” Noble. “Watt-hours tells you how long it will run, while watts tell you what it can run at all. Customers tend to fixate on capacity without looking at the continuous output.” With this in mind, we selected power stations with varying levels of watts and watt-hours. Customers tend to fixate on capacity without looking at the continuous output.” With this in mind, we selected power stations with varying levels of watts and watt-hours.

Rugged design: Portable power stations are well-suited for outdoor use. I highlighted stations with some level of dust, water and impact protection that can ideally handle different weather and environmental conditions.
Do solar-powered power banks really work?

Portable solar power banks combine the compact convenience of a power bank and the recharging capabilities of a solar panel. At least, on paper. In reality, portable solar power banks are far less efficient than separate power and solar equipment.

“All-in-one solutions like portable solar power banks go against everything I know about batteries, namely that batteries don’t like to get hot,” says Kreis. A regular power bank is much more convenient and effective for charging small electronics on the go, without the fuss of a solar panel. Solar panels are great for when you are truly off the grid, and don’t want to (or can’t) rely on, say, a vehicle to power your devices, says Kreis.
What is the difference between a portable power station and a solar generator?

A portable power station is essentially a large battery that can charge and power small and large devices  — think smartphones, speakers, microwaves and even refrigerators. A solar generator is typically a portable power station that includes a solar panel in the box or integrated into the station itself, says Kreis.

A solar-powered power station may be worth buying in addition to a regular one if you believe you’ll run out of battery based on what you use it for, according to Noble. “A station without a recharge source is destined to be merely an empty box until the grid comes back,” he says. “Solar panels can provide a renewable way to recharge your power station during extended outages or off-grid use. They’re especially beneficial if you’re facing anything from a multi-day hurricane outage to an extended camping trip.”

When buying a solar-power appliance, Noble recommends buying the panel as part of a set to make sure the voltage and wattage are both compatible with the station’s input range. “You’ll also want to set realistic expectations about your output,” he says. “For anyone relying on solar for emergency power, it’s best to size the battery as if the panels weren’t there and treat the panels as insurance.”
What is the difference between a power bank and a portable power station?

The main differences between a power bank and a portable power station have to do with what they’re meant to power and their level of voltage, according to Noble. “A power bank is a portable battery with USB ports, built with low-voltage DC power meant to top off your phone, tablet, and maybe your laptop,” he says. “Whereas a portable power station has an inverter that converts stored DC power into standard, 120-volt AC for actual wall outlets. That’s what allows you to plug in essential household items such as a refrigerator, sump pump, or CPAP machine, provided the power station is properly sized for the load.”
Frequently asked questions

If you’re often in situations where you have significant energy requirements without access to electricity — say, when running an RV or hefty home appliance at a camping site — then a portable power station could be well worth the investment. Additionally, portable power stations are safe to use indoors if you lose power during a natural disaster like a hurricane, unlike a gas generator, according to Noble.

“Gas generators need to be kept outside and away from windows as they produce carbon monoxide, not to mention the loud hum of the engine running,” he says. “But a power station has no engine, exhaust, or fuel. They run quietly and can be used indoors without the carbon monoxide concerns associated with gas generators. Power stations are also low maintenance, with no oil changes or pull cords necessary.”
Unlike a gas generator, which you can simply add more fuel to, a portable power station needs to be recharged from an electricity or solar source.

This largely depends on the station’s battery capacity and power output. Larger power stations have greater battery capacity and can theoretically run for longer, assuming you are powering similar devices. Portable power stations, like all rechargeable electronics, slowly lose capacity over time, so an older one may not run as long as a newer one.

title: Check your bathroom — you may have recalled hand soap sitting on your sink
summary: The FDA classified a recall of 2,696 cases of Intercon Chemical hand soap sold in 15 states after possible contamination with Pseudomonas and Serratia bacteria.
story: Before you reach for the hand soap by your sink, you might want to double check the bottle. Intercon Chemical Co. issued a voluntary recall for 2,696 cases of hand soap back on June 29 — and late last week, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) bumped that recall up to a Class II risk classification, which is the second-highest level they issue.
Six different products are on the list, and they were sold across 15 states. Keep reading to find out which states were affected and what this may mean for you.
Why was hand soap from Intercon Chemical Co. recalled?

Intercon Chemical Co., based in St. Louis, voluntarily recalled six hand soap products on June 29 after testing raised concerns about potential bacterial contamination. On September 11, the FDA classified the recall as Class II, meaning exposure to the affected soap could lead to temporary or medically reversible health effects.

Across the six recalled products, there is potential contamination with the following bacterial strains: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas putida, Pseudomonas monteilii, Serratia marcescens and Serratia nematodiphila. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Pseudomonas and Serratia bacteria are often associated with infections acquired in healthcare settings, though they’re naturally present in the environment, including in soil and water.
In total, the recall covers 2,696 cases of handsoap. The impacted hand soaps are listed below:

What to do if you have the recalled hand soap

If you have any of the six recalled products in your home or workplace, stop using them immediately. At this time, there is no information on whether or not Intercon is offering refunds to customers who purchased recalled hand soap.
Finally, if you’ve used the soap and start feeling unwell — even mildly — seek medical attention right away.
Other hand soaps to use instead

Just because the above hand soaps were recalled, doesn’t mean you should stop using hand soap all together. The below hand soaps are products NBC Selected has written about previously or ones that our editors love — none of which have been recalled at the time of publishing.
Softsoap Soothing Clean Aloe Liquid Hand Soap

NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin says that this aloe-scented hand soap is a personal favorite — she says the formula is hydrating and she appreciates how budget-friendly it is. Also nice: You can purchase large bottles of soap to refill the original dispenser, and refill bottles are recyclable once they’re empty.
Clean Cult Liquid Hand Soap Refills

Malin has also used Clean Cult’s hand soap to refill her dispensers. The soap comes in recyclable paper cartons and the formula contains aloe as well as essential oils. You can purchase the soap in scents like Sea Minerals, Lemon Verbena and Wild Lavender.
Aesop Resurrection Aromatique Hydrating Hand Wash

I love a fancy hand soap — it’s a little treat I give myself. This one from Aesop has been my pick lately. The scent is a combo of citrus and wood and the formula leaves my hands soft after washing. I also like how the sleek bottle looks great sitting on my bathroom sink.
Bath & Body Works White Tea & Sage Foaming Hand Soap

NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans has been using this soap for the last five years after a friend bought her a bundle as a housewarming gift. “I like that it’s mild enough that it doesn’t dry out my hands and leave my finger webs white and crispy, but it also makes my hands feel clean when I use it, especially after handling food,” she says. She buys the refill cartons and keeps a bottle on her bathroom sink and kitchen sink at all times.
Touchland Hand Sanitizer Spray

If you need to clean your hands on the go, this Touchland trio is a solid pick. The dye-free, hydrating spray doesn’t have the sticky residue of gel sanitizers, smells great and moisturizes skin. Just remember: Hand sanitizer isn’t a replacement for proper hand washing, but it’s a great backup when soap and water aren’t available.

title: October Prime Day dates were just announced — here’s everything you need to know

story: Amazon just confirmed that Prime Big Deal Days (unofficially dubbed October Prime Day 2026) is happening from October 6 to 7. When is October Prime Day?
October Prime Day 2026 is from October 6 to 7. Amazon previously hosted Prime Big Deal Days around these dates, so this timing is typical for the retailer.
What time does October Prime Day start?
October Prime Day starts at 12:01 a.m. PT on October 6 — that’s 3:01 a.m. ET, 2:01 a.m. CT and 1:01 a.m. MT.
When does October Prime Day end?
October Prime Day ends on October 7 at 11:59 p.m. PT — that’s October 8 at 2:59 a.m. ET, 1:59 a.m. CT and 12:59 a.m. MT.
How long is October Prime Day?
October Prime Day is 48 hours long. It’s shorter than Prime Day, which has been four days long since 2025 and typically happens in July (but took place in June in 2026).
Do you need to be a Prime member to shop October Prime Day deals?

Yes, only Prime members can take advantage of the deals during Prime Big Deal Days. You can sign up for a free 30-day trial Prime membership on Amazon’s website or app (learn about the three different types here). Amazon automatically charges you for your Prime membership once the free trial ends.

What is Prime Big Deal Days?

Prime Big Deal Days is Amazon’s second Prime Day-level sale of the year. The first one was in October 2022, and ever since, the retailer has hosted it around the same time each year. That’s why many people refer to Prime Big Deal Days as October Prime Day.

Like Prime Day, Prime Big Deal Days is exclusive to Prime members and offers some of Amazon’s lowest prices of the year across all product categories. But since the sale is in October rather than June or July, there’s an emphasis on early holiday shopping, so brands intentionally discount popular gifts like toys, gift cards, beauty sets and personal tech, as well as themed decor.
What is Amazon Prime?

Amazon Prime is the retailer’s loyalty membership program. You can get a free 30-day free trial, and after that, a standard membership costs $139 a year or $14.99 a month. Amazon also offers two types of discounted accounts: Prime for Young Adults, which is $7.49 a month for those 18 to 24 years old, and Prime Access, which is $3.50 for the first three months, and then $6.99 a month for those who qualify for certain government assistance programs.

Benefits of a Prime membership include exclusive savings during Prime Day and Prime Big Deal Days, as well as free two-day, one-day and same-day delivery. Prime members also get a handful of streaming and entertainment perks, plus they can order groceries online through Whole Foods or Amazon Fresh and sign up for a free Grubhub+ membership.
Is Prime Day twice a year?

Amazon has hosted two Prime Day-level events every year since 2022: Amazon Prime Day during the summer (typically July, but it was in June this year) and Prime Big Deal Days during the fall (typically in October, often referred to by shoppers as fall or October Prime Day). The retailer is following this schedule in 2026.
